title: Foods, drinks & dietary patterns
summary: How specific foods, drinks and eating patterns change systemic oxidative stress in humans. The biggest dietary levers are not 'antioxidant superfoods' but avoiding chronic overfeeding, large high-glycemic and high-fat meal spikes, alcohol, processed meat and high-heat dry cooking, inside a Mediterranean-style pattern. Among individual foods, high-phenolic extra-virgin olive oil, cruciferous foods that actually deliver sulforaphane (sprouts, seed powder with active myrosinase, raw or mustard-dressed broccoli), filtered coffee, blueberries, cocoa flavanols and brewed green tea have the best human evidence. Polyphenol milligrams and ORAC scores do not predict benefit: these compounds work through different routes (Nrf2 electrophile signalling, gut-microbial metabolites, endothelial nitric oxide, blunting NADPH oxidase), most show thresholds and plateaus, and very few human trials measure validated oxidative-damage markers.

factors.name: Broccoli sprouts (fresh, raw, chewed)
factors.headline: The richest whole-food source of glucoraphanin plus its own active myrosinase; daily sprout preparations reliably deliver sulforaphane and raised benzene detoxication by about 60% in randomized trials, but proof of lower oxidative damage or better clinical outcomes in healthy people is thin.

dose.effective: About 30-70 g fresh sprouts a day (a loose handful to roughly a cup), eaten raw and chewed well. In Qidong the effective beverage gave 600 µmol glucoraphanin + 40 µmol sulforaphane a day, and only a dose producing about 25 µmol of urinary sulforaphane metabolites per day clearly worked.
dose.studied_range: 16-200 g fresh sprouts per serving; 30 g/day for 10 weeks; 70 g/day (420 µmol glucoraphanin) for 8 weeks; 100 g/day for 3 days; sprout beverages 400-600 µmol glucoraphanin/day for 1-12 weeks.
dose.too_much: No toxicity at trial doses, including a 12-week thyroid safety analysis. Very large amounts are bitter and can cause bloating or loose stools.
dose.timeframe: Plasma sulforaphane peaks about 1-2 h after eating and falls with a half-life of about 2 h; detox-enzyme effects appear within days and held for 12 weeks without tolerance.
dose.notes: Chew thoroughly (chewing raised absorbed dose by about half vs swallowing whole). Do not cook: sprouts' own myrosinase is what makes them 3-4x better than glucoraphanin without enzyme. Glucoraphanin content varies by seed lot and cultivar; 70 g of the sprouts used in one trial held 420 µmol (about 6 µmol/g). Grow or buy from a reputable source, because raw sprouts carry a food-safety (bacterial) risk.

factors.mechanism: Chewing mixes glucoraphanin with myrosinase, releasing sulforaphane, a small electrophile that reacts with sensor cysteines on KEAP1 (notably C151). KEAP1 can then no longer tag Nrf2 for destruction, so Nrf2 accumulates and switches on ARE genes: NQO1, HO-1, GSTs, glutamate-cysteine ligase (glutathione synthesis), thioredoxin reductase. This is an indirect, catalytic antioxidant effect, not radical scavenging. Secondary actions seen in cells include reduced NF-kB DNA binding and HDAC inhibition (also seen in human blood cells after a sprout meal).
factors.interactions: Directly redundant in mechanism with [broccoli-seed-powder] and [sulforaphane-supplements]. Human data show absorption scales linearly from 25 to 200 µmol, a detox threshold near 25 µmol/day excreted, dose-dependent airway enzyme induction up to 200 g sprouts, and no tolerance over 12 weeks; but blood-cell markers did not rise further between 100 and 200 µmol/day. So adding sprouts on top of a large supplement dose probably gives diminishing Nrf2 returns, while adding them to a small dose probably helps. No human trial tests stacking. Sulforaphane is a far stronger and more bioavailable Nrf2 inducer than [turmeric-curcumin]; [coffee] and [aerobic-exercise-moderate] activate Nrf2 weakly and act through many other routes, so they are not made redundant. Mature [broccoli-mature] and [cruciferous-other] add fiber, folate, vitamin C and indole glucosinolates that sprouts lack.
factors.caveats: Many positive results are small or uncontrolled (e.g. lower IL-6 and CRP after 30 g/day for 10 weeks with no control group). Short sprout courses failed in asthma (100 g/day for 3 days), ozone-induced airway inflammation, and a calorie-challenge study, and 4 weeks of sulforaphane did nothing in COPD lungs. Conversion of any glucoraphanin that escapes plant myrosinase depends on gut bacteria and varies 1% to more than 40% between people. Benefits for hard outcomes are unproven.

factors.name: Broccoli seed powder / seed extract with active myrosinase
factors.headline: Seeds are the most concentrated glucoraphanin source; taken with their own (or added mustard) myrosinase they convert roughly 30-40% to sulforaphane, about double to quadruple glucoraphanin alone, but outcome trials with plain seed powder are scarce.

dose.effective: Enough assayed powder to supply roughly 100-200 µmol glucoraphanin a day with active enzyme, which at 30-40% conversion yields on the order of 30-80 µmol sulforaphane; this brackets the effective Qidong detox dose and the 50-150 µmol doses used in clinical trials.
dose.studied_range: Single doses of glucoraphanin-rich seed extract with or without myrosinase in bioavailability studies; seed-and-sprout extract tablets with myrosinase supplied the sulforaphane in several psychiatric trials (e.g. 100 µmol/day for 18 weeks).
dose.too_much: Not established. GI upset (nausea, loose stools) is the main dose-limiting effect of concentrated broccoli preparations.
dose.timeframe: Metabolites peak within hours and are mostly gone in 8-12 h, so effects are pulsatile with once-daily dosing.
dose.notes: Stir into cool or room-temperature water, yogurt or juice and wait a few minutes; never cook it. Less stomach acid (e.g. proton pump inhibitors) and enteric coating increased conversion in one pilot, suggesting acid can blunt plant myrosinase. A pinch of seed powder or mustard powder on cooked broccoli restores some conversion, the same principle as [mustard-seed-myrosinase]. Potency of bulk seed powder is rarely assayed.

factors.mechanism: Same KEAP1-Nrf2 electrophile mechanism as sprouts; the powder supplies both substrate (glucoraphanin) and enzyme (myrosinase). Without active myrosinase, conversion falls to whatever the person's gut bacteria (e.g. Bacteroides with the BT2159-2156 operon) can do.
factors.interactions: Mechanistically redundant with [broccoli-sprouts] and [sulforaphane-supplements]. Combining an enzyme-active source with a glucoraphanin-only source increases total delivery (65% vs 60% recovery, earlier peak). If seed powder already provides an effective dose, cooked [broccoli-mature] adds little extra sulforaphane but still adds fiber and micronutrients. See the saturation discussion in the deep-dive.
factors.caveats: Bioavailability data come from small volunteer groups. No trial has shown that seed powder lowers validated oxidative-damage markers (F2-isoprostanes, 8-oxo-dG) in healthy people. Bulk products vary and are seldom tested for glucoraphanin and enzyme activity.

factors.name: Mature broccoli (raw or lightly cooked)
factors.headline: Raw broccoli delivers roughly 3-10x more sulforaphane than fully cooked broccoli because cooking destroys myrosinase; high-glucoraphanin varieties lowered LDL cholesterol 5-7% in two RCTs, but glucoraphanin in supermarket heads varies more than 100-fold.

dose.effective: About 200 g (2 cups) raw or very lightly steamed, chopped and chewed well, or cooked broccoli with about 1 g mustard powder added after cooking. In trials 400 g/week of high-glucoraphanin broccoli lowered LDL.
dose.studied_range: 200 g single servings (pharmacokinetics); 400 g/week for 12 weeks (LDL trials); 200 g cooked + daikon daily for 15 days; 300 mL high-glucoraphanin soup weekly for 12 months.
dose.timeframe: Sulforaphane peaks about 1.6 h after raw and about 6 h after cooked broccoli; LDL effects over 12 weeks.
dose.notes: Raw: 32-37% of the potential isothiocyanate reaches the urine; steamed or cooked: 3.4-10%. Heating to about 60 °C can increase sulforaphane by inactivating epithiospecifier protein (which otherwise diverts glucoraphanin to an inactive nitrile), but 70 °C and above destroys floret myrosinase. Rough arithmetic: an average head (0.38 µmol/g) gives about 76 µmol glucoraphanin per 200 g, or about 28 µmol absorbed sulforaphane raw vs about 3 µmol fully cooked.

factors.mechanism: Nrf2 activation by sulforaphane plus fiber, folate, vitamin C and carotenoids. Mature heads also contain indole glucosinolates (yielding indole-3-carbinol and DIM), which sprouts largely lack and which act additively or synergistically with isothiocyanates on ARE genes in cell culture.
factors.interactions: If you already take a strong sulforaphane dose ([broccoli-seed-powder], [broccoli-sprouts], [sulforaphane-supplements]), cooked broccoli adds only a few µmol of extra sulforaphane, but raw broccoli can add a dose similar to the Qidong threshold, and the fiber, folate and indoles are not duplicated. Add [mustard-seed-myrosinase] when eating it cooked. Part of [high-fruit-vegetable-intake] and [mediterranean-diet] patterns.
factors.caveats: Head-to-head variation in glucoraphanin (<0.005 to 1.13 µmol/g) means any single serving may deliver little. Commercially frozen broccoli is blanched (heat-treated), so by the heating data it should be treated like cooked broccoli. Mortality associations for crucifers are observational.

factors.name: Mustard powder on cooked crucifers (myrosinase add-back)
factors.headline: Sprinkling 1 g powdered brown mustard on 200 g cooked broccoli raised sulforaphane metabolite excretion about 4.5-fold, and mustard-seed myrosinase doubled conversion of a broccoli seed extract (40% vs 19%).

dose.effective: About 1 g (roughly 1/2 teaspoon) powdered brown mustard per 200 g cooked broccoli, stirred in after cooking.
dose.studied_range: 1 g mustard powder with 200 g cooked broccoli (12 adults, crossover); mustard-seed powder with a glucoraphanin-rich seed extract (16 adults, crossover).
dose.timeframe: Same meal.
dose.notes: Add after cooking, once the food has cooled below steaming; heat inactivates mustard myrosinase too. Raw daikon radish (used to make Qidong's sulforaphane-rich beverage) or a pinch of broccoli seed powder works on the same principle.

factors.mechanism: Exogenous plant myrosinase hydrolyses glucoraphanin that survives cooking into sulforaphane in the meal and upper gut, instead of leaving it to variable colonic bacteria; then Nrf2 activation.
factors.interactions: Turns cooked [broccoli-mature] and [cruciferous-other] into meaningful sulforaphane sources and can boost glucoraphanin-only [sulforaphane-supplements]; same redundancy considerations as other Nrf2 inducers.
factors.caveats: Two small pharmacokinetic trials; no outcome data.

factors.name: Sulforaphane / broccoli extract supplements
factors.headline: Product type decides everything: glucoraphanin-only pills convert about 5-20% and very unevenly, whereas preformed (stabilised) sulforaphane or myrosinase-active products deliver about 40-70%; trials at 50-200 µmol/day show mixed results (modest glucose benefit in obese poorly controlled diabetes, small autism effects, several nulls).

dose.effective: Myrosinase-active or stabilised-sulforaphane products supplying roughly 40-150 µmol sulforaphane (about 7-27 mg) per day, the range used in most positive and negative trials.
dose.studied_range: 25-200 µmol/day sulforaphane-equivalent for 4 weeks to 12 months; up to ~340 µmol (60 mg) stabilised sulforaphane for 6 months; glucoraphanin 25-600 µmol/day.
dose.too_much: No serious toxicity in trials up to 200 µmol/day for weeks to months. GI effects (nausea, loose stools, reflux) are the main dose-limiting problem and contributed to drop-outs at 150 µmol/day and with 15-capsule regimens.
dose.timeframe: Hours per dose (pulsatile); clinical effects in trials appeared after 4-18 weeks and faded within weeks of stopping.
dose.notes: Check the label for active myrosinase or stabilised sulforaphane and an assayed µmol figure. A myrosinase-free supplement gave far lower isothiocyanates than 40 g fresh sprouts. Splitting the daily dose keeps blood levels up longer. Conversion is lower in people with higher body mass.

factors.mechanism: Nrf2 activation; human blood-cell HDAC inhibition after sprouts or glucoraphanin supplements in some studies; hepatic gluconeogenesis suppression via NRF2 in the diabetes work. Glucoraphanin without myrosinase depends on gut microbial activity, which antibiotics and bowel cleansing abolish.
factors.interactions: Redundant with [broccoli-sprouts] and [broccoli-seed-powder]. Poor microbial 'converters' gain most from myrosinase-active or preformed forms. Sulforaphane inhibited CYP3A4 and induced conjugating enzymes in human liver cells, and crucifer diets induce UGT1A1 in people: a theoretical interaction with drugs cleared by these enzymes at high supplement doses. In cancer patients, strong Nrf2 activation could theoretically protect tumour cells from chemotherapy; discuss with the oncologist. Not shown to add to [turmeric-curcumin] or [isolated-polyphenol-supplements].
factors.caveats: About half of registered sulforaphane trials remain unpublished. Effects in published trials are inconsistent: 150 µmol/day did not induce Nrf2 targets in COPD lungs; prediabetes trial missed its primary endpoint; autism trials in young children were null; prostate PSA trials missed primary endpoints. Commercial labels are often not independently verified. Long-term high-dose Nrf2 activation has open safety questions (synthetic activator bardoxolone raised heart-failure events).

factors.name: Other crucifers (kale, cabbage, Brussels sprouts, cauliflower)
factors.headline: Supply other isothiocyanates and indoles plus fiber and vitamins; in large cohorts the top fifth of crucifer intake had about 22% lower total mortality, and a controlled feeding trial lowered IL-6 by 19%, but oxidative-stress trials are few.

dose.effective: 1-2 servings (80-160 g) most days, some raw or lightly cooked; in a feeding trial a double dose (14 g/kg body weight, about 1 kg/day for a 70 kg adult) lowered IL-6.
dose.studied_range: Cohort intakes; feeding studies 7-14 g/kg body weight per day for 14 days.
dose.too_much: Collards, Brussels sprouts and some Russian kale can contain enough goitrin to reduce thyroid iodine uptake if eaten in very large amounts; with adequate iodine, normal intakes show no adverse thyroid effects.
dose.timeframe: Weeks.
dose.notes: Same cooking rules as broccoli: chop and wait, eat some raw, steam briefly, or add mustard powder after cooking.

factors.mechanism: Isothiocyanates (Nrf2), indoles, fiber and micronutrients; induction of conjugating enzymes such as UGT1A1 and GSTs.
factors.interactions: Overlaps with [broccoli-mature]; benefits from [mustard-seed-myrosinase] when cooked. Part of [high-fruit-vegetable-intake] and [mediterranean-diet].
factors.caveats: Inverse associations with mortality and cancers are observational and mostly rated weak to suggestive in an umbrella review.

factors.name: Blueberries
factors.headline: One cup (150 g) a day improved endothelial function over 6 months in metabolic syndrome, while half a cup did nothing; several trials show lower oxidized LDL, monocyte ROS or DNA oxidation.

dose.effective: 150 g fresh (1 cup) daily, or ~22-25 g freeze-dried powder.
dose.studied_range: 75-350 g fresh-equivalent/day for 6 weeks to 6 months; acute doses of 319-1791 mg blueberry polyphenols.
dose.timeframe: Acute FMD rise at 1-2 h and 6 h; chronic effects by 6-12 weeks.
dose.notes: Acute FMD rose with dose up to ~766 mg blueberry polyphenols and then plateaued. Frozen wild blueberries count. Juice with added sugar is not equivalent.

factors.mechanism: Anthocyanins are poorly absorbed intact; benefits track circulating phenolic metabolites (many made by gut bacteria) that lower neutrophil NADPH oxidase activity and improve nitric-oxide-dependent vasodilation. Not direct radical scavenging in plasma.
factors.interactions: Within-class saturation: little extra acute benefit above ~766 mg polyphenols per serving, so megadoses of berry extract are unlikely to add much. Mechanistically complementary to [broccoli-sprouts] (Nrf2) and [extra-virgin-olive-oil].
factors.caveats: Trials are small (n=18-115) and often industry-funded; oxidative-marker results are inconsistent across the 45 human studies reviewed, while vascular function results are the most consistent. A 75 g/day dose was ineffective. Insulin resistance, blood pressure and plasma thiols did not change in the 6-month trial. Cognitive trials are positive but small: a single 1-cup-equivalent wild blueberry drink preserved memory and executive function over 8 h in 35 middle-aged adults, and 6 months of powder improved processing speed in 86 older adults with mild cognitive decline.

factors.name: Blackberries
factors.headline: As rich in polyphenols as blueberries (mostly cyanidin-3-glucoside and ellagitannins), but the only human feeding trial measured fat oxidation and insulin sensitivity, not oxidative stress; benefits are inferred from other anthocyanin foods.

dose.effective: A 150 g serving is a reasonable berry portion by analogy with blueberry trials; 600 g/day was used in the one controlled feeding study.
dose.studied_range: 600 g/day for 7 days (1500 mg flavonoids/day).
dose.timeframe: Days to weeks.
dose.notes: Ellagitannins are converted by gut bacteria to urolithins, and people differ in whether they produce them.

factors.mechanism: Anthocyanin and ellagitannin metabolites (gut-derived phenolic acids, urolithins) acting on endothelium and inflammation.
factors.interactions: Interchangeable with [blueberries] and [berries-other] as a berry serving; little reason to think combining berries beyond ~1 cup/day adds much for oxidative stress.
factors.caveats: No RCT on oxidative-stress markers. In a 600 g/day feeding study blackberries lowered 24-h respiratory quotient and insulin AUC in overweight men.

factors.name: Other berries & cherries (strawberry, raspberry, chokeberry, blackcurrant, cranberry, cherries)
factors.headline: Berry RCTs pooled together show small improvements in LDL, systolic blood pressure, glucose and TNF-alpha, and anthocyanin foods improve flow-mediated dilation; specific oxidative-stress effects are inconsistent.

dose.effective: About 1 cup (150 g) of mixed berries daily, or ~3 servings per week in cohort data.
dose.studied_range: Juices, powders and whole fruit in 22 RCTs (1251 people); cranberry juice dose-response trials.
dose.timeframe: Acute (hours) for FMD; weeks for lipids and blood pressure.
dose.notes: Chokeberry and blackcurrant are far denser in anthocyanins than strawberries, but higher content has not been shown to give proportionally more benefit.

factors.mechanism: Anthocyanin and ellagitannin metabolites; vitamin C in strawberries.
factors.interactions: Substitutes for [blueberries]; not additive beyond plateau.
factors.caveats: Meta-analytic effects are small (LDL -0.21 mmol/L, SBP -2.7 mmHg) and heterogeneous. Cohort link: >3 servings/week of blueberries plus strawberries tended toward lower MI risk in young women (not significant on its own).

factors.name: Eggplant (skin: nasunin; flesh: chlorogenic acid)
factors.headline: Eggplant skin's nasunin is a strong superoxide scavenger and iron chelator in test tubes, and the flesh is rich in chlorogenic acid, but there is no human evidence that eggplant lowers oxidative stress.

dose.effective: No human dose for oxidative stress exists; eat it as a normal vegetable with the skin on.
dose.studied_range: One RCT used 1.2 g/day eggplant powder for 12 weeks (blood pressure outcome, attributed to acetylcholine, not antioxidants).
dose.timeframe: Unknown.
dose.notes: Phenol-Explorer has only a Folin value (61 mg/100 g) for whole purple eggplant. Chlorogenic acid is the dominant phenolic (>65% of phenolic acids) but content varies widely by cultivar and fruit segment. Frying in oil soaks up a lot of fat.

factors.mechanism: In vitro: nasunin (delphinidin-3-(p-coumaroylrutinoside)-5-glucoside) scavenges superoxide and inhibits hydroxyl radical generation mainly by chelating ferrous iron; chlorogenic acid is metabolised much like coffee chlorogenic acids.
factors.interactions: Chlorogenic acid overlaps with [coffee], which supplies far more per serving.
factors.caveats: The nasunin data are from rat brain homogenate and ESR assays at micromolar concentrations that dietary anthocyanins do not reach intact in human tissues. A 12-week RCT of eggplant powder lowered blood pressure in stressed adults, but the authors attribute it to choline esters (acetylcholine), not antioxidants.

factors.name: Coffee (paper-filtered)
factors.headline: The biggest single polyphenol (chlorogenic acid) source in many Western diets; RCTs at 3-4 cups/day cut background DNA strand breaks by about a quarter and urinary 8-iso-PGF2alpha by ~15%, and cohorts show the lowest mortality at 3-4 cups/day.

dose.effective: 3-4 cups (about 750 mL) per day of paper-filtered coffee.
dose.studied_range: 200-800 mL/day, from 8 hours to 4 weeks in intervention trials.
dose.too_much: Unfiltered coffee (French press, boiled, Turkish) raises LDL cholesterol through cafestol/kahweol; ~10 mg cafestol is in 2-3 cups of cafetiere coffee. Caffeine limits apply in pregnancy (see fertility sections).
dose.timeframe: DNA strand-break reduction detectable 2 h after the first cup; sustained at 4 weeks.
dose.notes: Paper filters retain the diterpenes. Decaffeinated coffee was also associated with lower mortality, so caffeine is not the whole story. Roast level shifts the compound mix (dark roast: less chlorogenic acid, more N-methylpyridinium).

factors.mechanism: Chlorogenic (caffeoylquinic) acids are partly absorbed in the small intestine and extensively metabolised by gut bacteria to dihydrocaffeic and ferulic acid derivatives; coffee also contains roast-derived compounds such as N-methylpyridinium. Trials show raised glutathione (consistent with induced antioxidant defences) and fewer DNA strand breaks rather than higher plasma 'antioxidant capacity'.
factors.interactions: Shares chlorogenic acids with [eggplant], [blueberries] and artichoke. Caffeine and fertility: covered elsewhere.
factors.caveats: Effects on plasma antioxidant capacity, antioxidant enzymes and lipid/protein damage are unclear across 26 intervention studies; the clearest signal is DNA protection and glutathione. Some positive trials were industry-sponsored. Pregnancy: high intake associated with low birth weight and pregnancy loss. When trying to conceive or pregnant, keep total caffeine under about 200 mg/day; see [caffeine-fertility].

factors.name: Green tea (brewed)
factors.headline: Four cups a day of decaffeinated green tea cut urinary 8-OHdG by 31% in heavy smokers over 4 months, and 4 cups/day lowered plasma MDA/HNE in metabolic syndrome; across 145 RCTs, flavan-3-ol foods including tea lower blood pressure by about 3/2 mmHg and improve FMD, while evidence on oxidative damage in healthy non-smokers stays weak.

dose.effective: About 4 cups (~1 L) per day of brewed green tea.
dose.studied_range: 4 cups/day for 8 weeks to 4 months.
dose.too_much: Brewed tea is considered safe at usual intakes (90-300 mg EGCG/day; heavy drinkers up to ~866 mg/day); rare idiosyncratic liver injury reported. See [green-tea-extract] for the supplement risk.
dose.timeframe: Weeks to months.
dose.notes: EGCG bioavailability is low and variable; plasma half-life ~3.4 h. Ring-fission valerolactone metabolites appear 3-15 h later.

factors.mechanism: Catechins (EGCG, EGC, EC) and their microbial valerolactone metabolites; at physiological doses mild Nrf2 signalling and effects on endothelium rather than plasma radical scavenging.
factors.interactions: Flavan-3-ols overlap with [cocoa-flavanols]. Tea with meals reduces non-heme iron absorption (relevant to [diet-iron-excess] and to iron-deficient people). Unlike high-dose vitamins C and E, 980 mg/day of green-tea polyphenols did not appear to blunt antioxidant-enzyme adaptation in sprinters.
factors.caveats: The smoker trial used decaf tea and showed no benefit for black tea. Smokers have high baseline oxidative damage, so the effect may not generalise. Concentrated extracts are a different exposure: free EGCG exposure rose by more than 60% after 4 weeks of 800 mg once-daily dosing, and in a 12-month RCT in 1021 women, high-dose green tea extract caused moderate or worse liver-test abnormalities in 5.1% (see [green-tea-extract]).

factors.name: Black tea
factors.headline: Black tea's catechins are largely converted to theaflavins and thearubigins; in the same smoker trial where green tea cut 8-OHdG, black tea had no effect, although in the UK Biobank drinking 2 or more cups a day was associated with 9-13% lower mortality.

dose.effective: No oxidative-stress benefit shown; normal intake (2-4 cups) is fine.
dose.studied_range: 4 cups/day for 4 months.
dose.notes: Folin values for black tea are similar to green tea, but the compounds differ.

factors.mechanism: Theaflavins/thearubigins and catechins, extensively metabolised by gut bacteria.
factors.interactions: Reduces non-heme iron absorption when taken with meals.
factors.caveats: Cohort associations with mortality and cardiovascular outcomes (UK Biobank, 498,043 adults) are observational; portion size and strength were not measured. Tea is one of the flavan-3-ol foods that lower blood pressure in pooled RCTs, but most of those trials used green tea or cocoa.

factors.name: High-dose green tea extract (EGCG pills)
factors.headline: EFSA (2018) concluded that 800 mg EGCG/day or more from supplements significantly raises liver transaminases in RCTs; extracts also cause rare severe liver injury, especially in multi-ingredient products.

dose.effective: No oxidative-stress benefit beyond brewed tea has been shown.
dose.studied_range: Supplements supply 5-1000 mg EGCG/day.
dose.too_much: >= 800 mg EGCG/day as a supplement (EFSA). Multi-ingredient products caused more severe injury.
dose.timeframe: Liver injury latency averaged ~6 months for green-tea-only products and ~6 weeks for multi-ingredient ones.
dose.notes: Brewed tea at traditional intakes is considered safe.

factors.mechanism: At high concentrations EGCG becomes pro-oxidant (generating H2O2) and hepatotoxic; patient susceptibility factors appear important.
factors.interactions: Do not combine with other hepatotoxic supplements.
factors.caveats: Absolute risk is low given wide use, but the dose threshold is clear from trials.

factors.name: Cocoa flavanols / high-flavanol dark chocolate
factors.headline: Cocoa flavanols reliably improve endothelial function (EFSA-authorised at 200 mg/day) and lower blood pressure in pooled RCTs; in the 21,442-person COSMOS trial, 500 mg/day did not significantly cut total CVD events (HR 0.90) or improve cognition overall, though memory improved in people with low habitual flavanol intake.

dose.effective: 200 mg cocoa flavanols/day: about 2.5 g high-flavanol cocoa powder or 10 g high-flavanol dark chocolate (EFSA).
dose.studied_range: 200-900 mg flavanols/day; COSMOS 500 mg/day (80 mg epicatechin) for a median 3.6 years.
dose.too_much: Chocolate brings sugar, fat and calories; extracts avoid these. Ordinary chocolate flavanol content varies widely and is rarely labelled.
dose.timeframe: FMD rises within hours; chronic improvement plateaued after ~2 weeks.
dose.notes: Epicatechin is the key active monomer; blood-pressure effects were larger above 50 mg epicatechin/day.

factors.mechanism: (-)-Epicatechin and its structurally related metabolites drive the vascular effect: an extract with 130 mg epicatechin improved FMD while a procyanidin-rich, low-epicatechin extract did not. They raise endothelial nitric oxide bioavailability and reduce NADPH-oxidase-driven superoxide; procyanidins are mostly degraded by gut bacteria to valerolactones. A high-flavanol drink prevented the post-meal and post-exercise rise in GC-MS F2-isoprostanes.
factors.interactions: Shares flavan-3-ols with [green-tea], apples and grapes; FMD gains appear regardless of dose in meta-analysis, implying a plateau.
factors.caveats: Most vascular trials are short and many were funded by cocoa companies. COSMOS primary endpoints (CVD events; memory at 1 year in COSMOS-Web; global cognition in COSMOS-Clinic) were null, and the CVD-death and low-flavanol memory findings are secondary or subgroup results. A 6-month PAD trial improved walking distance by 43 m but was a 44-person phase II study. Direct oxidative-damage markers are seldom measured.

factors.name: Extra-virgin olive oil (high-phenolic)
factors.headline: In the 200-man EUROLIVE RCT, oxidized LDL fell linearly with olive-oil phenolic content at 25 mL/day; EU law authorises an LDL-protection claim for oils supplying 5 mg hydroxytyrosol and derivatives per 20 g, and PREDIMED's EVOO arm cut major CVD events by ~30%.

dose.effective: 20-25 g (about 2 tablespoons) per day of a high-phenolic EVOO meeting >= 5 mg hydroxytyrosol + derivatives per 20 g.
dose.studied_range: 25 mL/day for 3 weeks (EUROLIVE); ~1 L/week per household in PREDIMED for years.
dose.too_much: Calories (about 120 kcal per tablespoon).
dose.timeframe: Measurable LDL changes within 3 weeks.
dose.notes: Use as the main culinary fat, raw on food or for moderate-heat cooking; phenolics decline with storage, light and heat. Refined olive oil has a fraction of the phenolics.

factors.mechanism: Hydroxytyrosol and its secoiridoid precursors (oleacein/3,4-DHPEA-EDA, oleuropein aglycone) bind to LDL and protect its lipids from oxidation; high oleic acid content makes membranes and LDL less oxidizable than PUFA-rich oils; modest Nrf2 and anti-inflammatory effects.
factors.interactions: Best evidence when it replaces butter, refined seed oils or [oxidized-frying-oils]. Improves carotenoid absorption from [tomatoes-lycopene] and [leafy-greens]. Core component of [mediterranean-diet].
factors.caveats: Short trials use LDL oxidation markers rather than outcomes; PREDIMED was re-analysed after randomisation irregularities (results held). Phenolic content varies enormously between oils and labels rarely state it. In the 50-person OLIVAUS crossover, 60 mL/day of high- vs low-polyphenol oil for 3 weeks gave no significant between-treatment difference, with oxLDL falling only within the high-polyphenol arm (more in abdominal obesity), so effects in healthy people are modest. The throat sting of fresh oil comes from oleocanthal, a COX inhibitor with ibuprofen-like activity in vitro; its clinical relevance at culinary doses is unknown.

factors.name: Walnuts and other nuts
factors.headline: A handful a day (30 g) lowers LDL and apoB and, in PREDIMED, cut major CVD events by ~28%; walnuts improved endothelial function, but direct oxidation markers were unchanged in several trials.

dose.effective: 30 g (a small handful) of mixed nuts or walnuts daily.
dose.studied_range: 30 g/day mixed nuts (PREDIMED); walnuts replacing ~32% of monounsaturated-fat energy for 4 weeks; 26 walnut trials (1059 people).
dose.too_much: Calories; walnut-enriched diets did not cause weight gain in trials.
dose.timeframe: 4 weeks for lipids and endothelial function.
dose.notes: Walnuts are rich in alpha-linolenic acid and gamma-tocopherol.

factors.mechanism: Lipid lowering (fewer oxidizable LDL particles), gamma-tocopherol, ellagitannins (converted to urolithins), ALA.
factors.interactions: Walnut PUFAs are oxidizable; store nuts cool and dark. Overlaps with [mediterranean-diet].
factors.caveats: In the walnut endothelial trial, oxidation biomarkers did not differ from the Mediterranean control diet; in PREDIMED the nut arm did not improve LDL oxidation traits (the EVOO arm did).

key_numbers.label: PREDIMED major CVD events HR, MedDiet + nuts

factors.name: Legumes (beans, lentils, chickpeas)
factors.headline: Good for glycemic control and fiber intake, which indirectly limits postprandial oxidative stress, but direct human oxidative-stress data are scarce; their very high Folin 'polyphenol' scores are largely an assay artefact.

dose.effective: About 1/2-1 cup cooked most days as part of a high-fiber pattern.
dose.studied_range: Part of dietary-pattern trials.
dose.notes: Black beans: Folin 1391 mg/100 g but only 54 mg/100 g by chromatography; lentils: Folin 3697 vs 10 mg/100 g. Folin reacts with proteins, sugars and other reducing substances.

factors.mechanism: Low glycemic load, fermentable fiber (short-chain fatty acids), modest polyphenols in seed coats.
factors.interactions: Replacing refined starch or processed meat with legumes reduces [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] and [processed-red-meat] exposure.
factors.caveats: Mostly inferred from fiber and dietary-pattern data.

factors.name: Whole grains
factors.headline: Each 90 g/day (3 servings) of whole grain is associated with ~19% lower CHD and 17% lower all-cause mortality; the oxidative-stress link is indirect, through lower glycemic spikes and fermentable fiber.

dose.effective: 3 servings (90 g) per day or more; associations continued up to ~210-225 g/day.
dose.studied_range: Cohort intakes; RCTs show lower body weight, blood pressure and cholesterol with higher fiber and whole grain.
dose.timeframe: Long-term.
dose.notes: Oats contain avenanthramides and beta-glucan; most grain phenolics (ferulic acid) are bound to fiber and released by gut bacteria.

factors.mechanism: Fiber-bound ferulic acid released in the colon, short-chain fatty acids, lower glycemic load.
factors.interactions: Replaces [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] carbohydrate.
factors.caveats: Observational for hard outcomes; refined grains and white rice showed little association.

key_numbers.label: CHD RR per 90 g/day whole grain

factors.name: Tomatoes and tomato products (cooked with oil)
factors.headline: Lycopene is 2.5-3.8x more bioavailable from tomato paste than fresh tomatoes and needs fat to be absorbed; tomato interventions lower LDL and IL-6, improve FMD, and blunted LDL oxidation after a high-fat meal.

dose.effective: A serving of cooked tomato product (sauce, paste, puree) with a little olive oil most days.
dose.studied_range: 21 intervention trials of tomato products or lycopene; single meals with processed tomato.
dose.timeframe: Postprandial (same meal) for oxLDL; weeks for lipids and FMD.
dose.notes: Tomato puree has ~8x the lycopene of raw tomato per 100 g (USDA). Fat-free dressing gave essentially no carotenoid absorption from salad.

factors.mechanism: Lycopene is a lipid-phase singlet-oxygen quencher carried in LDL; processing breaks cell walls and isomerises lycopene, improving absorption; tomato also supplies vitamin C and naringenin chalcone.
factors.interactions: Pair with [extra-virgin-olive-oil] or avocado; eat with high-fat meals to blunt postprandial oxidation.
factors.caveats: Lycopene supplements lowered systolic BP in pooled trials but tomato products, not pills, gave the lipid and FMD effects. Most trials are short.

key_numbers.label: Lycopene AUC, paste vs fresh tomato

factors.name: Carrots and carotenoid-rich vegetables (vs beta-carotene pills)
factors.headline: Carotenoid-rich foods are associated with lower oxidative DNA and lipid damage, but isolated beta-carotene supplements increased lung cancer and mortality in smokers (CARET), a textbook antioxidant paradox.

dose.effective: Regular orange/yellow and green vegetables eaten with some fat; a medium carrot (~60 g) provides ~5 mg beta-carotene.
dose.studied_range: Food: cohort and feeding studies. Supplements: 30 mg beta-carotene + 25,000 IU retinol daily (CARET).
dose.too_much: Beta-carotene supplements in smokers and asbestos-exposed workers: lung cancer RR 1.28, all-cause death RR 1.17. Beta-carotene supplements raised mortality in Cochrane analysis.
dose.notes: Absorption needs dietary fat: salads with full-fat dressing delivered much more carotenoid than reduced-fat or fat-free versions.

factors.mechanism: Carotenoids quench singlet oxygen and lipid peroxyl radicals in membranes and lipoproteins; at high doses in high-oxygen, smoke-exposed lungs beta-carotene can act as a pro-oxidant.
factors.interactions: Absorption improved by [extra-virgin-olive-oil], avocado.
factors.caveats: Food associations are observational. The supplement results are the reason not to translate food carotenoid data into pills.

factors.name: Leafy greens (spinach, lettuce, rocket, chard)
factors.headline: Nitrate-rich greens and beetroot lower systolic blood pressure by ~4 mmHg in short trials, and greens are the main dietary source of lutein; green leafy vegetables are among the produce most consistently linked to lower CVD and mortality.

dose.effective: 1-2 cups raw or 1/2-1 cup cooked daily.
dose.studied_range: Nitrate trials: 2 h to 15 days, dose-dependent BP effect.
dose.timeframe: Hours (nitrate) to weeks.
dose.notes: Nitrate effects on blood pressure were dose-dependent in meta-regression.

factors.mechanism: Nitrate -> nitrite -> nitric oxide supplements endothelial NO and can offset superoxide-driven NO loss; lutein and zeaxanthin protect membranes; folate.
factors.interactions: Nitrate and cocoa flavanols had additive effects on endothelial function at dietary amounts ([cocoa-flavanols]); pair greens with fat for carotenoid absorption ([extra-virgin-olive-oil]).
factors.caveats: Nitrate BP trials are short and small; oxidative-stress markers seldom measured.

key_numbers.label: Systolic BP change with inorganic nitrate/beetroot
Total polyphenols, chromatography, spinach (sum of compounds)

factors.name: Vitamin C foods (citrus, kiwi, peppers, strawberries)
factors.headline: Plasma vitamin C saturates near 200 mg/day (white cells saturate at 100 mg), easily reached from foods; extra beyond that is excreted and high-dose pills show no mortality benefit.

dose.effective: About 200 mg/day from food: e.g. 1 red pepper, or 2 kiwifruit, or 1 orange + 1 cup strawberries.
dose.studied_range: 30-2500 mg/day in depletion-repletion pharmacokinetics.
dose.too_much: Doses above ~400 mg/day have no evident value; at 1000 mg/day oxalate and urate excretion rise (kidney stone risk).
dose.timeframe: Steady state in 2-3 weeks.
dose.notes: Benefit is concentrated in people with low intake (smokers, low produce eaters).

factors.mechanism: Ascorbate is the main water-soluble chain-breaking antioxidant and regenerates vitamin E; kiwifruit also raised lymphocyte DNA resistance to H2O2 ex vivo beyond what its vitamin C explained.
factors.interactions: Vitamin C enhances non-heme iron absorption (good if iron-deficient; avoid iron + vitamin C supplements in iron overload, see [diet-iron-excess]). High-dose vitamin C + E blunted exercise adaptation (covered in exercise sections).
factors.caveats: In the Cochrane review vitamin C supplements had no effect on mortality; beta-carotene and vitamin E increased it.

key_numbers.label: Dose at which plasma vitamin C plateaus

factors.name: Garlic and onions
factors.headline: Garlic supplements lower blood pressure in hypertensives (about -8.7/-6.1 mmHg) and a meta-analysis of 12 small RCTs reports lower MDA and higher antioxidant enzymes, but these markers are weak and the trials low quality.

dose.effective: Culinary: 1-2 cloves/day crushed and left 10 min before cooking; supplement trials used aged garlic extract or powder.
dose.studied_range: 80-4000 mg/day garlic preparations for 2-24 weeks.
dose.too_much: Supplements can increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants.
dose.timeframe: Weeks.
dose.notes: Red onions are a major dietary source of quercetin (onion chromatography total ~140 mg/100 g in Phenol-Explorer).

factors.mechanism: Organosulfur compounds (allicin breakdown products, S-allylcysteine) activate Nrf2 and raise hydrogen sulfide signalling; onion quercetin.
factors.interactions: Another mild Nrf2 inducer; much weaker than sulforaphane.
factors.caveats: TAC and TBARS-type MDA are non-specific oxidative markers; effect sizes in the meta-analysis (Hedges' g up to 13.8) are implausibly large, a sign of small heterogeneous studies.

key_numbers.label: Onion (red), total polyphenols, chromatography (sum of compounds)

factors.name: Turmeric as a spice (culinary use)
factors.headline: A teaspoon (2-3 g) of ground turmeric holds roughly 60-100 mg curcumin, and eating it in food produces only nanomolar curcumin conjugates in blood (free curcumin mostly undetectable), so culinary turmeric is a pleasant spice with plausible gut-local effects but no demonstrated systemic antioxidant effect.

dose.effective: No proven systemic dose from cooking. Normal culinary use (about 1/2-2 teaspoons, 1.5-6 g ground turmeric/day in curries) is safe; one small haemodialysis trial used 2.5 g turmeric in juice three times a week.
dose.studied_range: Culinary-level feeding studies used a few grams of turmeric per meal; supplement trials use 80 mg-3 g/day of curcuminoids, mostly far above what food provides.
dose.too_much: Food amounts are within the EFSA ADI of 3 mg curcumin/kg/day (about 210 mg/day for a 70 kg adult). Turmeric is relatively high in soluble oxalate, a consideration for people with calcium-oxalate kidney stones. Cheap or imported ground turmeric can be adulterated with lead chromate.
dose.timeframe: Plasma conjugates peak about 30 min after a turmeric meal and persist for at least 8 h; no long-term human outcome data.
dose.notes: Pure turmeric powder averages about 3% curcumin by weight; most curry powders contain much less and vary widely. Black pepper and fat are often recommended, but in a head-to-head human study piperine-type adjuvants did not significantly raise curcumin exposure at a 207 mg dose. Buy from suppliers that test for lead; avoid unusually bright, cheap loose turmeric from markets with documented adulteration.

factors.mechanism: Curcumin is an alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl (Michael acceptor) that can modify KEAP1 Cys151 and activate Nrf2/HO-1 in cells, inhibits NF-kB signalling in vitro, and scavenges radicals in a test tube. In people, food doses are rapidly glucuronidated and sulfated in gut wall and liver; circulating forms are mainly conjugates that lack the parent compound's activity in cell assays. The gut lumen and intestinal wall are the only tissues likely to see meaningful concentrations.
factors.interactions: Redundant with, and far weaker than, food Nrf2 activators such as [broccoli-sprouts] and [broccoli-seed-powder]. Part of the general [herbs-spices] pattern within a [mediterranean-diet]-style or South Asian diet. Not interchangeable with [curcumin-supplements], which deliver 10-100x more curcuminoids in formulations designed to be absorbed. No known meaningful drug interactions at culinary amounts.
factors.caveats: Population associations (e.g. curry eaters with better cognitive scores in Singapore) cannot separate turmeric from the rest of diet and lifestyle. Claims that 'golden milk' or a pinch of pepper turns kitchen turmeric into a systemic antioxidant are not supported by pharmacokinetic data. In-vitro antioxidant capacity of turmeric says nothing about in-vivo effect. Lead chromate adulteration has been documented in turmeric from Bangladesh, India and Pakistan and has caused childhood lead poisoning in the US.

factors.name: Pomegranate juice
factors.headline: A famous 10-patient study reported dramatic falls in LDL oxidation and carotid thickness, but an 18-month RCT in 289 people found no effect on carotid progression and a meta-analysis found no lipid effect.

dose.effective: Not established; 240 mL/day was ineffective for carotid progression overall.
dose.studied_range: 50-240 mL/day for up to 3 years.
dose.too_much: Juice adds free sugar.
dose.notes: Punicalagins are converted by gut bacteria to urolithins, but people differ: across trials 25-80% make only urolithin A, 10-50% also make isourolithin A/urolithin B, and 5-25% make none, and the mix shifts with age. Purified urolithin A bypasses this (see [urolithin-a]).

factors.mechanism: Ellagitannins (punicalagin) -> ellagic acid -> urolithins; raised paraoxonase-1 in the small study.
factors.interactions: Ellagitannin source like [walnuts-nuts] and [blackberries]; downstream metabolite evidence is under [urolithin-a]. A pomegranate-plus-galangal extract increased motile sperm in one RCT (see [pomegranate-extract-sperm]).
factors.caveats: Industry-funded small studies drove early enthusiasm; possible benefit only in exploratory subgroups with high oxidative stress.

key_numbers.label: Total polyphenols, Folin assay, pure juice
People producing no urolithins (metabotype 0), range across trials

factors.name: Red wine and resveratrol
factors.headline: A glass of red wine contains well under 1 mg trans-resveratrol, oral resveratrol is almost entirely conjugated before it reaches blood, and urinary resveratrol levels did not predict mortality; the ethanol itself raises lipid peroxidation in a dose-dependent way.

dose.effective: No antioxidant reason to drink. If you drink, wine polyphenols taken with a fatty meal may limit postprandial lipid oxidation in the stomach (animal data).
dose.studied_range: Resveratrol supplements in trials range from tens to thousands of mg; a 25 mg oral dose left <5 ng/mL free resveratrol in plasma.
dose.too_much: Alcohol raises urinary isoprostanes dose-dependently; see [diet-alcohol].
dose.notes: Trans-resveratrol ~0.18 mg/100 mL (about 0.3 mg per 150 mL glass), so reaching supplement doses would take hundreds of glasses.

factors.mechanism: Resveratrol is absorbed (~70%) but rapidly sulfated and glucuronidated; wine's other polyphenols (anthocyanins, flavan-3-ols) are similar to those in grapes and berries without the ethanol.
factors.interactions: Ethanol counteracts the polyphenols; grapes, berries or dealcoholised wine provide the polyphenols without it. Supplement-dose resveratrol is covered under [resveratrol-pterostilbene-supplements]: meta-analyses find no overall blood-pressure effect and only trivial or very-low-certainty metabolic effects, and 250 mg/day blunted training gains in older men.
factors.caveats: Associations of urinary resveratrol metabolites with better lipids in PREDIMED are cross-sectional and confounded by wine drinking patterns.

key_numbers.label: Total polyphenols, chromatography, red wine (sum of compounds)
Free resveratrol in plasma after 25 mg oral dose

factors.name: Herbs and spices (oregano, rosemary, cloves, cinnamon, etc.)
factors.headline: Their biggest proven effect is in the pan: a polyphenol-rich spice mix cut malondialdehyde in cooked burgers by 71% and in the eaters' urine by 49%, and herb marinades cut heterocyclic amines in grilled steak by 57-88%.

dose.effective: Generous use in cooking, especially in meat dishes and marinades (about a tablespoon of dried herbs per meal); 14 g spice blend in a meal in one trial.
dose.studied_range: Single meals; marinating steaks 1 h before grilling at 204 °C.
dose.too_much: None established at culinary amounts.
dose.timeframe: Same meal.
dose.notes: Per gram, dried cloves, oregano and other herbs top every polyphenol table, but servings are small.

factors.mechanism: Rosmarinic acid, carnosic acid and carnosol inhibit lipid oxidation and Maillard/HCA chemistry in food and in the stomach, so fewer oxidized lipids are absorbed; a spice blend also lowered postprandial insulin and triglycerides.
factors.interactions: Counteracts [high-temperature-cooking] and [processed-red-meat] oxidation products. Here direct scavenging is plausible because the reaction happens in the food and gut, where concentrations are high.
factors.caveats: Meal studies are tiny (n=6-11) and short.

key_numbers.label: MDA reduction in spiced vs plain burger meat
Urinary MDA reduction after spiced burger
Total HCA reduction, Caribbean herb marinade

factors.name: Oily fish and omega-3 fats
factors.headline: Although EPA/DHA are highly peroxidizable, 3.4 g/day fish oil did not raise plasma F2-isoprostanes or MDA vs oleic or linoleic oils; long-chain omega-3s slightly reduce CHD events and lower triglycerides ~15%.

dose.effective: 1-2 servings of oily fish per week (salmon, sardines, mackerel), baked or poached rather than deep-fried.
dose.studied_range: 0.5 to >5 g/day long-chain omega-3 in RCTs (86 trials, 162,796 people).
dose.too_much: Cochrane found little or no effect of increased omega-3 on serious adverse events.
dose.timeframe: Weeks for triglycerides.
dose.notes: Oxidized (rancid) oils and deep-fried fish deliver dietary lipid oxidation products.

factors.mechanism: EPA/DHA alter membrane composition, eicosanoids and resolvins (anti-inflammatory); their double bonds are substrates for lipid peroxidation, so oxidized products in food or capsules matter more than the fats themselves.
factors.interactions: Eat with polyphenol-rich foods and avoid [oxidized-frying-oils]. TBARS rose with fish oil while F2-isoprostanes did not, illustrating how marker choice changes conclusions.
factors.caveats: Cochrane: little or no effect on all-cause mortality (RR 0.97) or total CV events; modest CHD reduction is low-certainty.

factors.name: Dietary fiber and the gut microbiome
factors.headline: Most dietary polyphenols reach the colon and only work after gut bacteria convert them, and people differ widely in this; a fiber intake of 25-29 g/day is linked to 15-30% lower mortality and cardiometabolic disease.

dose.effective: 25-29 g fiber/day or more from varied plants (whole grains, legumes, vegetables, fruit, nuts).
dose.studied_range: Cohorts (185 studies) and 58 RCTs.
dose.too_much: Increase gradually to limit bloating.
dose.timeframe: Microbiome shifts in days; outcomes long-term.
dose.notes: 'High' vs 'low excretor' and 'producer vs non-producer' metabotypes (urolithins, equol) explain part of why the same food works differently in different people.

factors.mechanism: Microbial catabolism turns anthocyanins, flavan-3-ols, chlorogenic acids and ellagitannins into smaller phenolic acids, valerolactones and urolithins that are absorbed and circulate for up to 48 h; fermentation yields short-chain fatty acids that support barrier integrity and lower inflammation.
factors.interactions: Determines how much benefit you get from [blueberries], [coffee], [cocoa-flavanols], [pomegranate], [walnuts-nuts], and how much glucoraphanin converts to sulforaphane ([sulforaphane-supplements]). Antibiotics abolish microbial glucoraphanin conversion.
factors.caveats: Mechanisms are well described; direct evidence that changing the microbiome lowers systemic oxidative stress in humans is limited.

key_numbers.label: Fiber intake with greatest risk reduction
Anthocyanin relative bioavailability incl. metabolites (13C tracer)

factors.name: Processed and red meat
factors.headline: IARC classifies processed meat as carcinogenic (Group 1) and red meat as probably carcinogenic (2A); heme iron catalyses lipid peroxidation and N-nitroso compound formation in the gut, with fecal N-nitroso compounds rising linearly with red-meat intake.

dose.effective: Keep processed meat rare and red meat to a few modest portions per week.
dose.studied_range: 0-420 g/day red meat in controlled feeding (dose-response for fecal N-nitroso compounds); white meat at 420-600 g/day had no effect.
dose.too_much: Each 50 g/day of processed meat raised colorectal cancer risk ~18% (IARC). Highest vs lowest heme intake: colon cancer RR 1.18.
dose.timeframe: Fecal markers change within days; cancer risk over years.
dose.notes: Meat eaten with red-wine polyphenols or polyphenol-rich spices produced less postprandial MDA in animal and human meal studies.

factors.mechanism: Heme iron catalyses peroxidation of dietary PUFA in the stomach and colon, producing malondialdehyde and 4-hydroxynonenal, and promotes endogenous N-nitrosation; processed meats add nitrite and pre-formed nitrosamines; high-heat cooking adds HCAs and PAHs.
factors.interactions: Worse with [high-temperature-cooking]; partly offset by [herbs-spices] and polyphenol-rich foods eaten in the same meal.
factors.caveats: Oxidative mechanism evidence is strongest for the gut lumen; effects on systemic markers are less studied. For sperm, only processed meat (not unprocessed red meat) has been linked to worse semen; see [unprocessed-red-meat].

key_numbers.label: Colon cancer RR, highest vs lowest heme iron
Fecal N-nitroso compounds per g red meat/day

factors.name: High-temperature dry cooking (AGEs, HCAs, PAHs)
factors.headline: Dry heat (grilling, broiling, roasting, frying) raises food AGEs 10-100-fold; a high-AGE meal cut flow-mediated dilation by 36% vs 21% for the same meal cooked gently, and a year on a low-AGE diet improved insulin resistance and oxidative stress markers.

dose.effective: Favour moist heat (stewing, poaching, steaming), lower temperatures and shorter times; marinate meat in acidic, herb-rich mixtures.
dose.studied_range: Single meals (15,100 vs 2,750 kU AGE); 1-year low-AGE diet in 138 obese adults with metabolic syndrome; 12 dietary AGE RCTs (293 people).
dose.too_much: Charred, well-done meat is the main HCA/PAH source.
dose.timeframe: Vascular effects within 2 h of a meal; metabolic effects over months.
dose.notes: Acidic ingredients (lemon juice, vinegar) and moist heat significantly reduced new AGE formation. Animal foods high in fat and protein are most AGE-prone; vegetables, fruit and whole grains stay low even when cooked.

factors.mechanism: Maillard reactions form AGEs (e.g. CML) that engage RAGE and activate NADPH oxidase and NF-kB; meat creatine + sugars + amino acids form heterocyclic amines; fat dripping on flames forms PAHs.
factors.interactions: Pairs with [processed-red-meat]; reduced by [herbs-spices] marinades; compounded by [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] (endogenous AGE formation).
factors.caveats: Many dietary-AGE trials come from one research group; measurement of food AGEs by ELISA is debated. The systematic review rated evidence as limited by trial quality.

key_numbers.label: FMD fall after high-AGE meal (vs 20.9% low-AGE)

factors.name: Repeatedly heated / oxidized frying oils
factors.headline: Reheating PUFA-rich oils generates lipid hydroperoxides and aldehydes that are partly absorbed; humans excrete more MDA after eating oxidized fat, and animal studies show raised blood pressure and vascular inflammation.

dose.effective: Avoid reused deep-frying oil and burnt or smoking oil; prefer EVOO or high-oleic oils for heat.
dose.studied_range: Mostly animal feeding studies; human postprandial studies.
dose.too_much: Repeatedly heated oil (common in fast food) is the main exposure.
dose.timeframe: Postprandial and chronic.
dose.notes: Polyphenols eaten in the same meal reduced stomach lipid peroxidation in animal models.

factors.mechanism: Thermal oxidation of linoleic and linolenic acids forms hydroperoxides, 4-hydroxynonenal, acrolein and other advanced lipid oxidation end-products that are absorbed and inflame the gut, liver and vessels.
factors.interactions: Worsens [processed-red-meat]; offset partly by [herbs-spices], [extra-virgin-olive-oil].
factors.caveats: Human outcome data are sparse; the evidence is largely mechanistic and from rodents.

factors.name: Industrial trans fats
factors.headline: Industrial trans fats raise LDL, lower HDL, promote systemic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction, and carry a higher coronary risk per gram than any other fat.

dose.effective: As close to zero as possible from partially hydrogenated oils.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts and controlled feeding studies.
dose.too_much: Any regular intake from partially hydrogenated oils.
dose.timeframe: Years.
dose.notes: Now banned or restricted in many countries; still present in some imported or older products.

factors.mechanism: Altered lipoprotein metabolism and inflammatory signalling (NF-kB), endothelial dysfunction.
factors.interactions: Often co-occurs with [oxidized-frying-oils] in fried fast food.
factors.caveats: The oxidative-stress component is one part of a broader cardiometabolic harm.

factors.name: Refined sugar and high-glycemic meals
factors.headline: A 75 g glucose drink more than doubled leukocyte ROS generation at 2 h in healthy people and lowered plasma vitamin E; large post-meal glucose and triglyceride spikes drive transient oxidative stress and endothelial dysfunction.

dose.effective: Limit sugary drinks and large refined-starch meals; pair carbohydrates with fiber, protein, fat and vinegar or acidic foods.
dose.studied_range: 75 g oral glucose; single high-fat or high-carbohydrate meals.
dose.too_much: Repeated large spikes; sugar-sweetened beverages.
dose.timeframe: Peaks at 1-3 h after the meal.
dose.notes: Cream (fat) and casein (protein) also raised leukocyte ROS, so the size of the meal matters, not only sugar.

factors.mechanism: Nutrient surges increase leukocyte NADPH oxidase (p47phox) and mitochondrial superoxide; hyperglycemia fuels AGE and polyol pathways and NF-kB activation.
factors.interactions: Additive with [diet-overfeeding]. Blunted by [whole-grains], [legumes], [dietary-fiber-microbiome] and polyphenol-rich foods with the meal (e.g. [tomatoes-lycopene], [herbs-spices]).
factors.caveats: Acute leukocyte ROS assays are not the same as chronic tissue damage; whether postprandial spikes in non-diabetic people cause disease independent of overall diet is debated.

key_numbers.label: Peak leukocyte (PMNL) ROS after 75 g glucose

factors.name: Excess calories / overfeeding and weight gain
factors.headline: Overeating by ~1000 kcal/day for 28 days raised urinary F2-isoprostanes and muscle protein carbonyls; 6000 kcal/day caused systemic oxidative stress within 2-3 days; BMI is one of the strongest correlates of urinary isoprostanes in the population.

dose.effective: Eat to energy balance; avoid sustained surplus.
dose.studied_range: +1040 kcal/day for 28 days; ~6000 kcal/day for 1 week.
dose.too_much: Any chronic surplus that drives weight gain, especially visceral fat.
dose.timeframe: Oxidative stress rises within days of overfeeding.
dose.notes: Avoiding a surplus probably outweighs any single 'antioxidant food'.

factors.mechanism: Nutrient excess overloads mitochondrial electron transport, increasing superoxide; adipose tissue oxidative stress carbonylated GLUT4, impairing insulin action; adipose inflammation.
factors.interactions: Reversed by [diet-calorie-restriction]; compounded by [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] and [diet-alcohol].
factors.caveats: Overfeeding studies are short and small; the Framingham link is cross-sectional.

key_numbers.label: Weight gain in 1 week at ~6000 kcal/day
Weight gain after 28 days at +1040 kcal/day

factors.name: Alcohol (dietary)
factors.headline: Acute alcohol raised urinary isoprostanes in a time- and dose-dependent way in healthy volunteers, tracking blood alcohol; red-wine polyphenols do not cancel this.

dose.effective: Less is better for oxidative stress; there is no antioxidant reason to drink.
dose.studied_range: Acute doses in a randomized placebo-controlled study; patients with alcoholic liver disease.
dose.too_much: Dose-dependent; heavy and binge drinking worst.
dose.timeframe: Hours.
dose.notes: Covered in more depth in the lifestyle section.

factors.mechanism: Ethanol metabolism by CYP2E1 generates ROS; acetaldehyde depletes glutathione; raised NADH/NAD+ alters mitochondrial redox; iron mobilisation.
factors.interactions: Negates the polyphenol benefit of [red-wine-resveratrol].
factors.caveats: Small acute study; chronic moderate intake data are confounded.

factors.name: Mediterranean diet
factors.headline: In PREDIMED (7447 high-risk adults) a Mediterranean diet with EVOO or nuts cut major CVD events by ~30%; sub-studies found larger falls in urinary 8-oxo-dG, more oxidation-resistant LDL and borderline lower F2-isoprostanes vs a low-fat diet.

dose.effective: Daily EVOO as the main fat, vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains, nuts (about 30 g), fish weekly, little red/processed meat or sweets.
dose.studied_range: 4.8 years median (PREDIMED); 1-year oxidative sub-studies.
dose.timeframe: Oxidative markers improved at 1 year; CVD events diverged within a few years.
dose.notes: The wine component is optional and not needed for the benefits.

factors.mechanism: Combines olive phenolics (LDL protection), high produce and fiber (gut metabolites), lower glycemic load, fewer AGEs and processed meats, and better fatty-acid profile.
factors.interactions: Contains most of the beneficial foods here; individual 'superfoods' add little on top of it.
factors.caveats: PREDIMED was retracted and republished after randomisation irregularities; re-analysed results held. Oxidative endpoints were secondary and in subsamples.

key_numbers.label: LDL oxidative modifications, EVOO arm vs control

factors.name: DASH diet
factors.headline: In obese hypertensive adults DASH lowered blood pressure by ~8/7 mmHg, raised plasma antioxidant capacity and prevented the F2-isoprostane rise during an experimental lipid infusion.

dose.effective: 8-10 servings/day of fruit and vegetables, low-fat dairy, whole grains, nuts and legumes, low sodium and sweets.
dose.studied_range: 4 weeks per diet in a 24-person crossover study.
dose.timeframe: 4 weeks.
dose.notes: Blood pressure benefits of DASH are well established in larger trials; oxidative data are small.

factors.mechanism: High potassium, fiber and plant polyphenols; reduced sodium lowers vascular NADPH oxidase activity.
factors.interactions: Overlaps heavily with [high-fruit-vegetable-intake] and [mediterranean-diet].
factors.caveats: Oxidative-stress data come from one small study.

factors.name: High fruit and vegetable intake
factors.headline: Doubling produce from 5.8 to 12 servings/day for 2 weeks reduced lymphocyte 8-OHdG and urinary isoprostanes, but another controlled trial found 600 g/day had no effect on oxidative DNA damage in healthy non-smokers; cohorts show lower mortality up to ~800 g/day.

dose.effective: At least 5 servings (400-500 g)/day, ideally up to ~800 g, from diverse botanical families.
dose.studied_range: 600 g/day for 24 days; 12 servings/day for 14 days.
dose.timeframe: Weeks.
dose.notes: Diversity across plant families mattered in the positive trial; benefit was larger in people with low baseline carotenoids.

factors.mechanism: Many compounds acting through different routes (Nrf2 electrophiles, gut metabolites, vitamin C/carotenoids, nitrate, fiber, potassium).
factors.interactions: The null Danish trial suggests healthy people with adequate defences may already be near a ceiling for oxidative DNA damage.
factors.caveats: Oxidative-marker trials conflict; cohort benefits may partly reflect healthier lifestyles.

key_numbers.label: All-cause mortality RR per 200 g/day fruit and vegetables

factors.name: Calorie restriction
factors.headline: In CALERIE, the only long-term RCT of calorie restriction in healthy non-obese adults, prescribed 25% CR (about 12% achieved) for 2 years lowered urinary F2-isoprostanes by 13-27%, LDL, blood pressure, CRP and insulin resistance, at the cost of some bone and lean mass.

dose.effective: A sustained moderate deficit of ~10-15% of energy needs; CALERIE participants achieved 11.9% (about 300 kcal/day) and lost ~7.5 kg.
dose.studied_range: 25% CR prescribed for 6 months to 2 years in non-obese and overweight adults.
dose.too_much: Bone density fell at spine and hip and fat-free mass fell ~2.2 kg over 2 years in CALERIE; extreme CR risks malnutrition and amenorrhoea. Not for underweight people, pregnancy or eating disorders.
dose.timeframe: Isoprostane reductions present at 12 months and sustained at 24 months; DNA damage reduced at 6 months.
dose.notes: In overweight people weight loss itself drives much of the effect. Long-term CR does not lower IGF-1 in humans unless protein intake also falls (~0.95 g/kg/day).

factors.mechanism: Lower energy flux reduces mitochondrial ROS production per day (metabolic adaptation of 80-120 kcal/day beyond weight loss, lower T3), lower insulin signalling, less adipose inflammation, and hormetic upregulation of defences.
factors.interactions: Opposite of [diet-overfeeding]. The comparator against which all fasting protocols should be judged: [time-restricted-eating], [alternate-day-fasting] and [five-two-diet] match but do not beat it when calories are equal. Combine with [resistance-training] and adequate protein and calcium to protect bone and lean mass. Overlaps with [weight-loss].
factors.caveats: Long-term adherence is hard; most people benefit from avoiding surplus rather than strict CR. Effects on DNA-methylation aging clocks were small (DunedinPACE only). Lean, active women risk crossing into low energy availability; see [vigorous-exercise-low-energy].

factors.name: Intermittent fasting (umbrella: TRE, alternate-day, 5:2, periodic)
factors.headline: Intermittent fasting helps mainly by making people eat less: across 99 RCTs it beat ad libitum eating, but matched calorie restriction about equally (Cochrane: -0.56 kg difference over 3-12 months), and calorie-matched trials show no fasting-specific drop in oxidative stress markers.

dose.effective: Any form you can sustain that produces a modest energy deficit: an 8-10 h daily eating window, alternate-day fasting (~500 kcal or zero on fast days), or 2 days/week of 500-600 kcal (5:2). See [time-restricted-eating], [alternate-day-fasting], [five-two-diet].
dose.studied_range: Daily fasts of 12-20 h, 24-36 h alternate-day fasts, 2 days/week at ~25% of needs, for 3 weeks to 12 months.
dose.too_much: Daily eating windows under ~6 h and multi-day fasts increase lean-mass loss; not for pregnancy, eating disorders, underweight, type 1 diabetes, or insulin/sulfonylurea users without medical adjustment.
dose.timeframe: Weight and insulin changes within 4-12 weeks; oxidative stress markers follow weight loss.
dose.notes: Fasting length matters physiologically (ketones barely rise before ~20 h), but for health outcomes the total energy deficit matters far more than the pattern.

factors.mechanism: Energy deficit and weight loss lower insulin, adipose inflammation and mitochondrial ROS production. Longer fasts add a metabolic switch to fatty acids and ketones; beta-hydroxybutyrate can inhibit class I HDACs and induce FOXO3A and metallothionein (mouse data). Early eating windows align intake with circadian insulin sensitivity.
factors.interactions: Effects largely overlap with [diet-calorie-restriction] and [weight-loss]; benefits are biggest with [excess-adiposity] and [glycemic-control] problems. Pair with [resistance-training] and adequate protein to limit lean loss. Diet quality still matters: fasting does not offset [diet-overfeeding] on eating days. Late, short windows can shorten sleep; see [short-sleep].
factors.caveats: Most claims about autophagy, 'cellular cleanup' and longevity come from rodents. Calorie-matched trials (Templeman 2021, Liu 2022, Peters 2025) found no fasting-specific benefit. Only modified alternate-day fasting for BMI reached high-quality evidence in an umbrella review, and IF is associated with fat-free mass loss. The early eTRF oxidative stress result (n = 8) was driven partly by worsening on the control schedule.

key_numbers.label: IF vs continuous restriction, weight at 3-12 months (Cochrane)
ADF vs continuous restriction, weight (network meta-analysis)

factors.name: Curcumin supplements (enhanced-bioavailability extracts)
factors.headline: Enhanced-absorption curcumin (micellar, cyclodextrin, phytosome, colloidal) modestly lowers CRP (~0.6 mg/L) and MDA and reduces knee-osteoarthritis pain about as much as an NSAID in short trials, but the trial base is small, heterogeneous and low quality, and rare idiosyncratic liver injury is now well documented.

dose.effective: Osteoarthritis: 1500 mg/day Curcuma extract (the ibuprofen-comparison trial) or ~180 mg/day curcumin as Theracurmin, for 4-12 weeks. Biomarkers: ~600 mg/day curcuminoids or more (often with piperine) for at least 4-8 weeks; micellar or gamma-cyclodextrin forms deliver more curcumin per mg.
dose.studied_range: 80 mg/day (nanomicelle) to 8 g/day (standard powder) in trials; single doses up to 12 g tolerated.
dose.too_much: EFSA ADI 3 mg/kg/day (about 210 mg/day at 70 kg), which many products exceed. Liver injury (hepatocellular or cholestatic hepatitis, latency 1-4 months, one US death) has been linked to high-dose, high-bioavailability products and is strongly associated with HLA-B*35:01; 3 of 7 implicated US products also contained piperine. GI upset at gram doses.
dose.timeframe: Pain effects within 2-8 weeks; biomarker changes at 4-12 weeks; fasting plasma curcuminoids reached ~50 nmol/L after 3 weeks of meal-time micellar dosing.
dose.notes: Free (unconjugated) curcumin is barely detectable in blood even with advanced formulations; most 'fold-increase' claims compare total conjugates after enzymatic hydrolysis and use different assays, so brand comparisons are not reliable. Best head-to-head data favour micelles (57-185x) and gamma-cyclodextrin (30-39x); phytosome ~8-29x; piperine adds little to conjugate exposure in the head-to-head study but inhibits drug-metabolising enzymes. Take with meals.

factors.mechanism: Claimed: Nrf2 activation via KEAP1 Cys151 (Michael acceptor), NF-kB inhibition, direct radical scavenging and iron chelation. Reality check: these effects appear in cells at 1-20 uM, whereas oral dosing gives low-nanomolar free curcumin and mostly glucuronide/sulfate conjugates that are inactive in cell assays. Curcumin also degrades rapidly and is a known pan-assay interference compound, so many in-vitro 'hits' are suspect. Clinical effects that do appear (OA pain, CRP) may come from gut-local actions, minor metabolites, or bias, and the mechanism in humans is not established.
factors.interactions: Overlaps with [sulforaphane-supplements], [broccoli-sprouts] and [broccoli-seed-powder] on Nrf2; sulforaphane is far more potent and bioavailable, and there are no human data on combining them, so adding curcumin for Nrf2 is likely redundant (inference). Its distinct use case is symptomatic osteoarthritis pain. No human evidence that curcumin blunts training adaptations the way high-dose vitamins C/E do ([antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]); this is untested rather than disproven. Pharmacokinetic interactions: curcumin inhibits intestinal BCRP (sulfasalazine exposure up 3.2x) and CYP/P-gp in vitro; piperine raises phenytoin levels. Short studies found no change in INR on warfarin or bleeding time on antiplatelets, but caution is still advised with anticoagulants. Belongs to the broader [isolated-polyphenol-supplements] category.
factors.caveats: The field carries an integrity problem: a leading curcumin laboratory has dozens of retracted papers, and one glycaemic meta-analysis was itself retracted. Most positive trials are small, short, single-centre and often from a few research networks; meta-analyses show very high heterogeneity and GRADE certainty is low. Larger or Western trials are frequently null (FAP adenomas, radiation dermatitis, prostate cancer, Alzheimer's disease, micellar curcumin on CRP/lipids). Liver injury is rare but real; stop and test liver enzymes if jaundice, dark urine or fatigue appear. Avoid with gallstones or bile-duct obstruction (curcumin contracts the gallbladder), with marginal iron stores (iron chelation in mice), and in pregnancy (no safety data at supplement doses).
