factors.name: Urolithin A (supplement; gut metabolite of ellagitannins in pomegranate, berries, walnuts)
factors.headline: In company-funded RCTs, 500-1000 mg/day of urolithin A for 1-4 months improved muscle endurance or strength (about 12% for leg strength) and lowered CRP and acylcarnitines in older and middle-aged adults, but most primary endpoints were not met and trained runners gained no performance.

dose.effective: 500-1000 mg/day purified urolithin A (the Mitopure product in all major trials).
dose.studied_range: 250-1000 mg/day for 4 weeks to 4 months.
dose.too_much: No safety signal up to 1000 mg/day for 4 months; long-term data lacking.
dose.timeframe: Plasma and muscle biomarker changes by 4 weeks; muscle endurance differences at 2 months.
dose.notes: Ellagitannin foods only yield urolithin A if your gut bacteria can make it: across trials 5-25% of people make none and 10-50% partly divert to isourolithin A/urolithin B, and the distribution shifts with age. Taking urolithin A directly bypasses this metabotype problem.

factors.mechanism: Urolithin A, made by gut bacteria from ellagic acid, induces mitophagy (selective removal of damaged mitochondria) and mitochondrial gene expression; it is not a meaningful radical scavenger at the concentrations reached in plasma.
factors.interactions: Food precursors overlap [pomegranate], [walnuts-nuts], [blackberries] and [berries-other], but only help producers. Unlike high-dose vitamins C and E, there is no sign that it blunts training adaptations; in trained runners it lowered creatine kinase.
factors.caveats: All major human trials were sponsored by the manufacturer. In the 66-person JAMA Network Open trial the primary endpoints (6-minute walk, maximal muscle ATP production) were null; in the middle-aged trial peak power (primary) was null. Oxidative-damage markers have not been measured directly. The immune study reports 4-week changes in cell phenotypes, not infections.

key_numbers.label: Leg muscle strength gain, middle-aged adults (4 months)
People producing no urolithins (metabotype 0), upper bound across trials

factors.name: Fisetin (senolytic flavonol supplement; traces in strawberries)
factors.headline: Fisetin cleared senescent cells and extended lifespan in one mouse study, but the NIA Interventions Testing Program found no lifespan extension and no placebo-controlled senolytic trial in humans has reported results; food supplies milligrams, while trials test about 1.4 g doses.

dose.effective: None established.
dose.studied_range: Senolytic trials: 20 mg/kg/day for 2 consecutive days (about 1.4 g for a 70 kg adult), repeated intermittently; one small continuous trial used 200 mg/day for 12 weeks.
dose.too_much: High-dose human safety data are limited; flavonols alter the bioavailability of some drugs (see [quercetin]).
dose.notes: All flavonols and flavones together averaged about 17 mg/day in a Japanese diet, so eating strawberries cannot approach trial doses.

factors.mechanism: In cell and mouse models fisetin triggers apoptosis of senescent cells by disabling their anti-apoptotic defences, lowering the inflammatory SASP. Any antioxidant action in vivo is weak and short-lived.
factors.interactions: Same flavonol class as [quercetin]. The human senolytic data so far come from dasatinib plus quercetin, a drug combination, not from fisetin.
factors.caveats: The widely quoted mouse lifespan result was not reproduced by the multi-site ITP. The Mayo AFFIRM-LITE trial (started 2018) is still listed as enrolling in 2026. Senescent cells also help wound healing, so clearing them is not risk-free. The only completed RCTs are a small trial in obese men measuring adipokines and an unrelated stroke trial.

key_numbers.label: Total flavonol + flavone intake, Japanese women

factors.name: Quercetin (supplement; onions, capers, apples, tea)
factors.headline: At 500 mg/day or more, quercetin lowers blood pressure by about 4/3 mmHg in pooled RCTs, but it did not reduce colds in a 1002-person trial, improves endurance by a trivial ~2%, and left oxidative-stress markers unchanged even when it lowered blood pressure.

dose.effective: 500-1000 mg/day for blood-pressure effects.
dose.studied_range: 100-1250 mg/day for 2-12 weeks; senolytic protocols used 1000-1250 mg for 3 days with dasatinib.
dose.too_much: Long-term safety above 1000 mg/day beyond 12 weeks is not established; quercetin alters the bioavailability of some drugs, and animal data raise kidney concerns.
dose.timeframe: Blood pressure change within 4 weeks.
dose.notes: Quercetin glucosides from onions were 52% absorbed vs 24% for the aglycone used in most pills; almost all circulates as conjugates.

factors.mechanism: Quercetin conjugates act on vascular signalling (nitric oxide availability, NADPH oxidase) rather than by scavenging radicals in plasma; in senolytic regimens it is paired with the kinase inhibitor dasatinib.
factors.interactions: Same flavonol class as [fisetin]. Flavonol foods overlap [green-tea], [black-tea] and onions in [garlic-alliums]. Unlike resveratrol, 1000 mg/day for 2 weeks did not blunt mitochondrial markers in untrained men (see [resveratrol-pterostilbene-supplements]).
factors.caveats: The often-quoted '~1% bioavailability' understates absorption from onion glucosides, but plasma levels stay low-micromolar. The infection benefit appeared only in a post-hoc subgroup. Dasatinib plus quercetin trials are small and mostly open-label; the one RCT (bone) missed its primary endpoint, and quercetin was not detected in CSF in the Alzheimer's pilot.

factors.name: Spermidine (wheat germ, soy, legumes, mushrooms, aged cheese; supplements)
factors.headline: Higher dietary spermidine tracked with 24% lower mortality per standard deviation in an Austrian cohort, but the only long human trial (12 months of 0.9 mg/day wheat-germ extract) found no memory or biomarker benefit, so the autophagy story is still animal-based.

dose.effective: Not established.
dose.studied_range: About 0.9 mg/day spermidine from wheat-germ extract for 3-12 months.
dose.too_much: No safety concerns at the supplement doses studied.
dose.timeframe: 3-12 months studied.
dose.notes: Supplement doses are small next to total dietary polyamines (Swedish adolescents ate about 316 umol/day of all polyamines, half from fruit). Whole foods are the practical source.

factors.mechanism: Spermidine lowers protein acetylation and induces autophagy; in mice its cardioprotection disappeared when cardiomyocyte autophagy (Atg5) was knocked out. It has no meaningful direct antioxidant role.
factors.interactions: Autophagy induction overlaps conceptually with [diet-calorie-restriction]. Spermidine-rich foods overlap [legumes] and [whole-grains], which confound the cohort association.
factors.caveats: The cohort cannot separate spermidine from the whole-grain, legume and vegetable pattern it marks. The 3-month pilot's benefit (confidence interval touching zero) did not replicate in the 12-month trial. Polyamines support cell growth; long-term cancer implications in humans are unstudied.

key_numbers.label: All-cause mortality HR per 1-SD higher intake

factors.name: Moringa leaf powder (moringin and related isothiocyanates)
factors.headline: Moringa leaves make unusually stable isothiocyanates, and 20 g of leaf powder blunted a post-meal glucose rise in people with diabetes, but a 2025 meta-analysis of 9 RCTs found no consistent effect on glucose, lipids or weight (very low certainty).

dose.effective: Not established; the acute glucose effect used 20 g leaf powder with a meal, and 4 g raised insulin secretion in healthy adults.
dose.studied_range: 1-20 g leaf powder; chronic RCTs of 2 weeks or more.
dose.too_much: Large doses are unpalatable; supplement isothiocyanate content is rarely stated.
dose.timeframe: Acute post-meal effects; chronic effects unproven.
dose.notes: Fresh leaves crushed in water let the leaf's own myrosinase form moringa isothiocyanates, which kept about 80% of their activity after 30 days at 37 C, far more stable than sulforaphane.

factors.mechanism: Moringa isothiocyanates are electrophilic Nrf2 activators and NF-kB/iNOS inhibitors in cells; in mice they suppressed liver gluconeogenesis. The leaf's polyphenols, fibre and minerals may also contribute to glucose effects.
factors.interactions: Same electrophile/Nrf2 route as [broccoli-sprouts] and [watercress-peitc]; stacking them mostly targets one pathway.
factors.caveats: Claims that moringin equals or beats sulforaphane rest on cell assays; there are no published human pharmacokinetic or Nrf2-target data for moringin. Continuous-glucose-monitor anecdotes are not trials. Human RCTs are small and heterogeneous.

key_numbers.label: Insulin secretion rise after 4 g leaf powder

factors.name: Watercress (phenethyl isothiocyanate, PEITC)
factors.headline: 85 g/day of raw watercress for 8 weeks cut lymphocyte DNA damage by 17% (oxidative purine damage by 24%, more in smokers), and watercress or pure PEITC shifted a tobacco lung carcinogen toward detoxification in smokers.

dose.effective: About 85 g (a large bowl) of raw watercress daily.
dose.studied_range: 85-170 g/day for 3 days to 8 weeks; pure PEITC 40 mg/day for 1 week.
dose.timeframe: Carcinogen-metabolism shift within 2-3 days; DNA-damage changes at 8 weeks.
dose.notes: Eat raw or barely wilted so chewing releases PEITC via the plant's myrosinase. Watercress also doubled plasma lutein and raised beta-carotene, so not all of the effect is PEITC.

factors.mechanism: PEITC inhibits cytochrome P450 activation of the tobacco nitrosamine NNK and, like other isothiocyanates, conjugates glutathione and activates Nrf2-driven phase II enzymes; the carotenoids add lipid-phase antioxidant capacity.
factors.interactions: Same pathway family as [broccoli-sprouts], [cruciferous-other] and [moringa]. The carotenoid boost overlaps [leafy-greens].
factors.caveats: Trials are small; in the 82-smoker PEITC trial the change in carcinogen activation was only 7.7%. The exercise study had 10 men. There are no cancer-outcome data.

key_numbers.label: Urinary detoxified NNK metabolites in smokers
NNK activation ratio with 40 mg/day PEITC

factors.name: Indole-3-carbinol (I3C) and DIM supplements
factors.headline: I3C (200-400 mg/day) and DIM reliably shift estrogen metabolism toward 2-hydroxylation, and I3C regressed cervical precancer in one 30-woman trial, but no trial shows fewer cancers, DIM lowered active tamoxifen metabolites, and high-dose I3C caused liver tumours in male mice and uterine cancer in female rats.

dose.effective: No outcome-based dose; 200-400 mg/day I3C or 300 mg/day DIM shifted estrogen metabolites.
dose.studied_range: I3C 200-1200 mg/day; DIM 150 mg twice daily for up to 12 months.
dose.too_much: Do not combine with tamoxifen (endoxifen fell). NTP found carcinogenicity at high gavage doses. DIM plasma levels plateau above about 1000 mg I3C.
dose.timeframe: Estrogen metabolite shift within 1 month.
dose.notes: I3C itself never reaches the blood; it condenses in stomach acid, and DIM is the only product detected in plasma. Eating crucifers gives a much smaller version of the same shift.

factors.mechanism: Acid-condensation products of I3C (chiefly DIM) activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor and induce CYP1A enzymes that hydroxylate estradiol at C-2 rather than C-16; they are also weak Nrf2 inducers.
factors.interactions: Synergistic or additive with isothiocyanates (sulforaphane, PEITC) in cell Nrf2 assays. Food sources overlap [cruciferous-other] and [broccoli-mature]. Drug interaction with tamoxifen.
factors.caveats: The urinary 2:16-hydroxyestrone ratio is a surrogate with an uncertain link to cancer risk. The cervical trial is small and unreplicated. Higher catechol-estrogen levels could have long-term downsides. Marketing for 'estrogen detox' outruns the data.

key_numbers.label: Complete CIN regression on I3C (8 of 17) vs placebo (0 of 10)
Plasma DIM Cmax plateau (1000 mg I3C)

factors.name: Wasabi, horseradish and mustard (allyl and other short-chain isothiocyanates)
factors.headline: Pungent condiments supply isothiocyanates that are well absorbed (in animals) and concentrate in urine, and one 72-person RCT found a wasabi 6-MSITC extract improved memory in older adults, but there are no human oxidative-stress or disease trials.

dose.effective: Not established; culinary amounts.
dose.studied_range: Wasabi 6-MSITC supplement for 12 weeks; cabbage meals for allyl isothiocyanate kinetics.
dose.too_much: Large amounts irritate the gut.
dose.notes: Isothiocyanates form only when the plant's myrosinase acts on crushed tissue, so freshly grated root or prepared mustard delivers them; lightly cooked cabbage gave more allyl isothiocyanate than fully cooked.

factors.mechanism: Allyl isothiocyanate and 6-MSITC are electrophiles that conjugate glutathione and activate Nrf2; allyl isothiocyanate is excreted as an N-acetylcysteine conjugate concentrated in urine.
factors.interactions: Mustard powder also restores myrosinase activity to cooked broccoli: see [mustard-seed-myrosinase]. Same pathway as [broccoli-sprouts] and [watercress-peitc].
factors.caveats: Bioavailability figures for allyl isothiocyanate come mainly from animals. The memory trial is a single study with improvement in 2 of several cognitive domains. Erucin (rocket) and sulforaphene (radish) have essentially no human outcome data.

factors.name: Resveratrol and pterostilbene supplements
factors.headline: Despite the sirtuin story, resveratrol supplements show trivial or very-low-certainty metabolic effects in meta-analyses, 250 mg/day blunted training gains in older men, and pterostilbene 250 mg/day lowered blood pressure but raised LDL by 17 mg/dL.

dose.effective: None established for health outcomes.
dose.studied_range: Resveratrol 10 mg to 2 g/day; pterostilbene 100-250 mg/day for 6-8 weeks.
dose.too_much: Gram doses cause nausea, diarrhoea and weight loss. Avoid around training if adaptation is the goal. See [egg-resveratrol] for embryo-transfer concerns.
dose.timeframe: Weeks.
dose.notes: Food supplies well under 1 mg/day (see [red-wine-resveratrol]); supplements are a pharmacological, not dietary, exposure.

factors.mechanism: Resveratrol activates AMPK and indirectly SIRT1 and acts as a mild hormetic stressor at low micromolar levels; in muscle it can dampen the reactive-oxygen signalling that drives training adaptation.
factors.interactions: Can antagonise exercise adaptation (contrast [quercetin], which did not blunt mitochondrial markers short-term). Part of the broader [isolated-polyphenol-supplements] picture.
factors.caveats: Positive single trials exist (150 mg/day in 11 obese men; 200 mg/day for memory; 500 mg/day augmenting muscle response to training in 65-80-year-olds), but other trials were null, and in the 52-week Alzheimer's trial (up to 1 g twice daily) brain-volume loss was greater on resveratrol. Exercise results conflict by age, dose and training type.

key_numbers.label: VO2max gain blunted by 250 mg/day during training
LDL change, pterostilbene 125 mg twice daily
Systolic BP change, pterostilbene 125 mg twice daily

factors.name: Astaxanthin (supplement; also in salmon, krill and Haematococcus algae)
factors.headline: In 12 small RCTs astaxanthin lowered blood MDA (SMD -0.95) and IL-6 in type 2 diabetes, and 2-8 mg/day reduced a DNA-damage marker in young women, but CRP and TNF-alpha did not change and no clinical outcomes have been tested.

dose.effective: 2-12 mg/day in trials.
dose.studied_range: 2-12 mg/day for 4 weeks to 3 months.
dose.too_much: No safety signal at these doses; long-term data limited.
dose.timeframe: 4-12 weeks.
dose.notes: Fat-soluble carotenoid; capsules produced dose-dependent rises in plasma astaxanthin.

factors.mechanism: A polar xanthophyll that sits across lipid membranes and quenches lipid peroxyl radicals and singlet oxygen there, a setting where direct scavenging is plausible; it also raised Nrf2 targets (HO-1, NQO1) in human granulosa cells.
factors.interactions: Fertility data in [astaxanthin-sperm] and [astaxanthin-egg]. In the NIA ITP, astaxanthin extended male (not female) median mouse lifespan by 12%.
factors.caveats: Trials are small and short and mostly use soft markers (TBARS-type MDA, total antioxidant capacity); heterogeneity is high.

factors.name: Citrus flavanones (hesperidin: oranges, orange juice, supplements)
factors.headline: 500 mg/day hesperidin or 500 mL/day orange juice lowered diastolic blood pressure and improved endothelial function in small crossover trials, and a meta-analysis finds modest lipid, glucose and systolic BP effects above 500 mg/day.

dose.effective: 500 mg/day hesperidin, or 500 mL/day orange juice.
dose.studied_range: Hesperidin 500 mg/day or more for 3 weeks to over 12 weeks.
dose.too_much: Juice adds free sugar; whole oranges are a better default.
dose.timeframe: 3-4 weeks for blood pressure and FMD; over 12 weeks for lipids.
dose.notes: Hesperidin carries a sugar that gut bacteria must remove before absorption, so responses vary between people.

factors.mechanism: Hesperetin metabolites stimulate endothelial nitric oxide synthase (via Akt/AMPK, H2O2-dependent signalling in endothelial cells) and reduce adhesion-molecule expression.
factors.interactions: Vascular route overlaps [cocoa-flavanols]; oranges also count toward [vitamin-c-foods].
factors.caveats: Trials are small and short; the FMD benefit was shown in metabolic syndrome; most supplement trials are not independently replicated.

key_numbers.label: FMD on hesperidin vs placebo (metabolic syndrome)

factors.name: Ground flaxseed (lignans plus alpha-linolenic acid)
factors.headline: 30 g/day of milled flaxseed for 6 months lowered systolic blood pressure by about 10 mmHg (15 mmHg in hypertensives) in a 110-patient RCT, one of the largest blood-pressure effects of any food; lignans and ALA both appear to contribute.

dose.effective: 30 g/day milled flaxseed (roughly 3-4 tablespoons).
dose.studied_range: 30 g/day in foods for 6 months.
dose.timeframe: Months.
dose.notes: Use milled seed; enterolignans rose 2-50-fold on the milled-flax diet.

factors.mechanism: Secoisolariciresinol diglucoside is converted by gut bacteria to enterodiol and enterolactone; ALA and its oxylipins also lower blood pressure. Plasma ALA tracked systolic and diastolic pressure, lignans tracked diastolic.
factors.interactions: ALA overlaps only partly with [diet-omega3-fish]. Lignans also come from [whole-grains]. In PREDIMED, lignan intake was among the subclasses most strongly linked to lower mortality.
factors.caveats: One main RCT, in peripheral artery disease patients; replication in the general population is limited. Enterolactone production depends on the microbiome.

factors.name: Soy foods and isoflavones (equol producers vs non-producers)
factors.headline: Soy isoflavones do not change male sex hormones (41-study meta-analysis), and only 25-60% of people carry gut bacteria that convert daidzein to the more potent equol, one likely reason soy trials disagree.

dose.effective: Food amounts; no oxidative-stress dose established.
dose.studied_range: Male hormone trials used soy protein or isoflavone extracts across a wide dose range.
dose.notes: Equol production is a microbiome trait; non-producers get less estrogenic activity from the same soy.

factors.mechanism: Isoflavones are weak estrogen-receptor ligands; equol, made only by some microbiomes, binds more strongly. In-vivo antioxidant effects are not established.
factors.interactions: See [soy-sperm] (no effect on male fertility measures) and [soy-isoflavones-egg] for the ART cohort.
factors.caveats: Few trials stratify by equol status, and oxidative-stress outcomes are rarely measured.

key_numbers.label: Share of people able to produce equol

factors.name: Ketogenic diet (nutritional ketosis)
factors.headline: Cutting carbohydrate to roughly 20-50 g/day raises blood beta-hydroxybutyrate to about 0.5-3 mmol/L; it is a proven epilepsy therapy and lowers HbA1c, triglycerides and CRP in the short term, but direct evidence that it lowers oxidative damage in humans is thin, and LDL/apoB can rise sharply in lean people.

dose.effective: Under ~20-50 g/day total carbohydrate (about 5-10% of energy), protein around 1.2-2 g/kg, fat to appetite; aim for blood BHB 0.5-3 mmol/L. Build it around non-starchy vegetables, olive oil, nuts, seeds, fish, eggs and avocado rather than processed meat and butter.
dose.studied_range: Epilepsy: classic 4:1 diet or modified Atkins 10-20 g/day carbohydrate for >= 3 months. Type 2 diabetes: < 20-50 g/day for 6 months to 5 years. Weight/metabolic trials: 2 weeks to 2 years.
dose.too_much: Ketoacidosis needs BHB >= 3 mmol/L plus acidosis; healthy people on diet alone rarely exceed ~3 mmol/L, but SGLT2-inhibitor users, people with type 1 diabetes, and breastfeeding women can tip into ketoacidosis. Not for pregnancy or trying to conceive without specialist care, fatty-acid oxidation disorders, pyruvate carboxylase deficiency, porphyria, eating disorders, or people on insulin or sulfonylureas without medication adjustment.
dose.timeframe: Ketones rise within days (a fast alone gives ~1 mmol/L by 24-48 h), and stable ketosis was confirmed at ~4 weeks in one RCT. Muscle fat-oxidation adaptation takes 5-6 days to a few weeks, glycaemic effects take weeks, and seizure benefit is judged at ~3 months.
dose.notes: Fingerstick blood BHB is the reference measurement. Breath acetone is a reasonable non-invasive proxy. Urine strips read only acetoacetate, fade as the kidney adapts, and are best in early-morning or post-dinner urine. Check lipids including apoB at baseline and 6-12 weeks.

factors.mechanism: Low insulin releases fatty acids that the liver converts to acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB). In cells and mice, BHB inhibits class I HDACs, which up-regulates FOXO3a, MT2, catalase and MnSOD. This result failed to replicate in one cell study. BHB also blocks NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and activates HCAR2 (GPR109A). Ketone oxidation shifts the mitochondrial NAD and coenzyme Q redox couples. In rats, ketogenic feeding causes a brief burst of mitochondrial H2O2 and 4-HNE that activates Nrf2 and raises glutathione, which looks like hormesis. In humans the clearer routes are lower glucose and insulin, fewer glycaemic excursions, weight loss and lower triglycerides. High fatty-acid supply can raise mitochondrial H2O2 emission, and acetoacetate can generate superoxide in vitro.
factors.interactions: Overlaps heavily with [diet-calorie-restriction] and [diet-intermittent-fasting] because all three raise ketones and cause weight loss. Most metabolic benefit runs through [weight-loss] and better [glycemic-control], and through removing [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] foods. Against [mediterranean-diet], the crossover trial found equal HbA1c, but keto raised LDL and cut fibre. A Mediterranean-style keto (olive oil, fish, vegetables) is the reasonable middle ground. Usually lowers fibre and bifidobacteria, working against [dietary-fiber-microbiome]. Impairs high-intensity endurance economy, so it is a poor fit for competitive [hiit-vigorous-exercise] or racing; [aerobic-exercise-moderate] and [resistance-training] are maintained. BHB and sulforaphane ([broccoli-sprouts]) both act on HDACs and Nrf2 in lab models. That overlap is an inference: no human data show synergy or redundancy. In PCOS see [ketogenic-diet-egg]. For a less restrictive option see [low-carb-diet].
factors.caveats: Human oxidative-stress data are small and short. In 20 women, 2 weeks raised total antioxidant status but did not change MDA, SOD or catalase. Children on the diet had higher brain glutathione, but that study was cross-sectional. In an isocaloric metabolic-ward study keto did not speed fat loss, and in an inpatient crossover people ate ~690 kcal/day more on animal-based keto than on a plant-based low-fat diet. Weight-loss advantage over low-fat diets is about 1 kg at a year. Diabetes benefits are largest at 3-6 months and fade by 12 months in RCT pooling. The Virta data are non-randomised. LDL rose about 41 mg/dL in lean people and fell in people with BMI >= 35. The 'lean mass hyper-responder' coronary-plaque data are cross-sectional, and the follow-up paper that claimed apoB did not predict plaque progression was retracted in 2026. Animal-based low-carb patterns are associated with higher mortality and plant-based ones with lower. Other risks: kidney stones (~6%), thiamine, folate, magnesium and iodine gaps, constipation, and poorer bone-turnover markers in athletes. Unhealthy versions (processed meat, little fibre) undo much of the case.

factors.name: Moderate low-carbohydrate diet (non-ketogenic, ~50-130 g/day)
factors.headline: Cutting carbohydrate to under ~130 g/day (below ~26% of energy) without necessarily reaching ketosis lowers HbA1c, triglycerides and CRP over 3-6 months about as well as keto for many people. Weight loss matches low-fat diets at 12 months, and plant-based versions are linked to lower mortality.

dose.effective: About 50-130 g/day of carbohydrate, mostly from vegetables, legumes, nuts, berries and some intact whole grains, replacing refined starch and sugar. Protein and unsaturated fat fill the gap.
dose.studied_range: RCTs of < 130 g/day (or < 26-45% of energy) for 3-24 months; DIETFITS reached ~30% of energy from carbohydrate for 12 months.
dose.too_much: Below ~50 g/day it becomes a ketogenic diet, with the risks listed there. Patterns heavy in animal fat and processed meat are linked to higher mortality.
dose.timeframe: Glycaemic and triglyceride effects within weeks; benefits in diabetes trials shrink by 12 months unless adherence holds.
dose.notes: This is mostly the carbohydrate-quality message ([refined-sugar-high-glycemic]) plus some quantity restriction. It keeps the fibre and polyphenols that strict keto tends to drop.

factors.mechanism: Lower glycaemic load means smaller post-meal glucose and insulin spikes. That means less glucose-driven NADPH oxidase activation and less AGE formation, plus lower triglycerides and liver fat. Benefits on oxidative and inflammatory markers mostly track weight loss and glycaemic control rather than ketones.
factors.interactions: Largely the same benefit as [glycemic-control] and [weight-loss]. Compatible with [mediterranean-diet] and [dietary-fiber-microbiome]. In PCOS, low-carbohydrate diets were the best dietary subgroup for reproductive outcomes (see [ketogenic-diet-egg]). A stricter version is [ketogenic-diet].
factors.caveats: In DIETFITS (609 adults), healthy low-carb and healthy low-fat diets gave the same 12-month weight loss. Lipid responses vary, and LDL can rise. The mortality data are observational, and the result depends on what replaces the carbohydrate.

factors.name: Exogenous ketones (ketone esters, ketone salts, MCT/C8 oil)
factors.headline: A ketone-ester drink raises blood BHB to ~2-4 mmol/L within an hour, and salts or C8 oil raise it much less. Acute doses lower glucose by ~0.5 mmol/L and give a small cognitive benefit, but they do not improve exercise performance, and the anti-inflammatory story is contradictory in humans.

dose.effective: Ketone monoester ~0.3-0.5 g/kg (about 12-27 g BHB) gives a peak BHB of ~2.8-4 mmol/L for 2-4 h. Ketone salts ~12-24 g BHB give ~1 mmol/L. C8 (tricaprylin) 20 mL twice daily gives ~0.3-0.5 mmol/L. A 15 g twice-daily MCT drink was used in the 6-month MCI trial.
dose.studied_range: Single doses up to 714 mg/kg monoester; 25 mL (26.8 g) monoester three times daily for 28 days in healthy adults; 12 g BHB before meals for 14 days in obesity; 30 g/day MCT for 6 months.
dose.too_much: Gut upset (nausea, cramps, diarrhoea) at high doses, worse with salts and MCT. Salts carry a large sodium/potassium load and half the BHB is the less useful L-isomer. Avoid with SGLT2 inhibitors or type 1 diabetes without medical advice.
dose.timeframe: Peak at 30-60 min, back to baseline within 3-4 h; no lasting ketosis without repeated dosing.
dose.notes: A meal cuts the peak by about a third. Ketone esters taste harsh and cost several dollars per serving at retail (a market observation, not from a study). They give ketones without carbohydrate restriction, so they do not reproduce the low-insulin, weight-loss and low-glucose milieu of the diet.

factors.mechanism: Supplies D-BHB directly. In the short term it lowers hepatic glucose output, free fatty acids and lipolysis (HCAR2), and gives the brain an alternative fuel. HDAC inhibition and NLRP3 blockade are cell and mouse findings. In humans, a single dose increased monocyte caspase-1 activation, while 14 days of pre-meal dosing decreased it.
factors.interactions: No human trials measure oxidative-damage markers. It does not replace [ketogenic-diet] for epilepsy. Glucose lowering adds to diabetes drugs. For athletes, pre-race ketone drinks impaired a time trial; post-session ester during overload training is the one positive signal.
factors.caveats: A meta-analysis of 13 RCTs found no performance effect (g = -0.05). The cognitive meta-analysis effect is small (SMD 0.29) across heterogeneous trials. Most trials are industry-linked, small and short. Vendor claims about 'burning fat' are backwards: exogenous BHB suppresses lipolysis.

key_numbers.label: Peak BHB, ketone salts (same BHB dose)

factors.name: Time-restricted eating (8-10 h eating window)
factors.headline: Eating within an 8-10 h window cuts intake by roughly 170-550 kcal/day and gives weight loss similar to calorie counting; when calories are matched (Liu 2022 NEJM, Peters 2025) it adds little or nothing, and 4-6 h windows lowered 8-isoprostane ~35% only alongside ~3% weight loss.

dose.effective: An 8-10 h daily window, ideally early (e.g., 8:00-16:00 or 7:00-15:00), at least 5-6 days/week, for 12 weeks or more.
dose.studied_range: 4-10 h windows, early (ending 14:00-16:00), mid-day or late (12:00-20:00), 4 days to 12 months.
dose.too_much: Windows of 4-6 h increased lean-mass loss (6-h TRE: -1.5 kg lean in 8 weeks); 16:8 without resistance training reduced appendicular lean mass. An observational NHANES analysis linked <8 h eating to CV mortality (HR 2.35) but is heavily confounded.
dose.timeframe: Glucose and insulin changes within 4 days to 5 weeks; weight loss over 3-12 months.
dose.notes: Early windows look better than late ones in some trials (Xie 2022) but not when calories are held constant (Peters 2025). The overnight fast in a 16:8 schedule barely raises ketones (~0.1-0.15 mmol/L).

factors.mechanism: Mainly spontaneous energy reduction. Early windows align meals with daytime insulin sensitivity and lower evening glucose exposure; a longer overnight fast lowers insulin and slightly raises fat oxidation and ketones. eTRF raised blood SIRT1 and LC3A expression in one 4-day study.
factors.interactions: Equivalent to [diet-calorie-restriction] at matched intake; benefits track [weight-loss]. Combine with [resistance-training] and ~1.6 g/kg protein to keep lean mass. Late windows that push dinner close to bedtime may conflict with [short-sleep] and [shift-work-circadian]. Useful as a weight-loss tool in [pcos].
factors.caveats: Many trials are small and short. TREAT (Lowe 2020) found 16:8 alone no better than three meals. Manoogian 2024 found only a -0.10% HbA1c effect in metabolic syndrome. The 2024 AHA abstract (published as Chen 2025) used two days of dietary recall; the <8 h group was ~2% of participants, more often smokers, food-insecure and habitual breakfast-skippers, and the CV association lost significance when <8 h was required on both recall days (HR 1.78, 0.85-3.74).

factors.name: Alternate-day fasting
factors.headline: Fasting (0-25% of needs) every other day gives the same 1-year weight loss as daily 25% restriction (-6.0% vs -5.3%), with more dropouts; calorie-matched ADF did not lower oxidative stress markers and lost less fat than daily restriction.

dose.effective: Fast days at ~500 kcal (about 25% of needs) or zero calories, alternating with ad libitum or ~125% days, for 8 weeks to 12 months.
dose.studied_range: 20-36 h fasts every other day; 3 weeks to 1 year.
dose.too_much: Persistent hunger on fast days and high dropout (38% at 1 year). Hypoglycaemia risk with insulin or sulfonylureas.
dose.timeframe: Weight and insulin changes within 3-8 weeks.
dose.notes: Strict 36-h fasts raise beta-hydroxybutyrate even on eating days; a 20-h fast barely does (0.10 mmol/L).

factors.mechanism: Energy deficit plus repeated 20-36 h fasts that lower insulin and raise fat oxidation and ketones; in a long-term cohort ADF lowered sICAM-1, LDL and T3.
factors.interactions: Matches [diet-calorie-restriction] and [five-two-diet]; benefits follow [weight-loss]. Food quality on eating days still matters; a [mediterranean-diet]-style pattern is a sensible base.
factors.caveats: The large falls in isoprostanes, carbonyls and nitrotyrosine (Johnson 2007) came from an uncontrolled study of 10 people. Templeman 2021: ADF without a deficit did nothing, and with a deficit lost less fat than daily CR. The network meta-analysis edge for ADF (-1.29 kg) is trivial.

factors.name: 5:2 diet (two low-calorie days per week)
factors.headline: Two days/week at 500-650 kcal matched continuous restriction for weight loss (-6.4 vs -5.6 kg at 6 months; -8.0 vs -9.0 kg at 1 year) and for HbA1c in type 2 diabetes, with more hunger and double the hypoglycaemia rate on glucose-lowering drugs.

dose.effective: 500 kcal (women) / 600 kcal (men) on 2 non-consecutive days per week, usual healthy eating on the other 5.
dose.studied_range: 400-650 kcal on 2 days/week for 3-12 months.
dose.too_much: Not for insulin or sulfonylurea users without medication adjustment (hypoglycaemia RR 2.05); not for pregnancy or eating disorders.
dose.timeframe: Weight changes within 1-3 months.
dose.notes: Low-calorie days do not usually produce deep ketosis because some food is eaten.

factors.mechanism: Weekly energy deficit with two short periods of very low intake; small extra falls in fasting insulin vs continuous restriction in one trial.
factors.interactions: Interchangeable with [diet-calorie-restriction] and [alternate-day-fasting]; choose by preference. Benefits follow [weight-loss] and [glycemic-control].
factors.caveats: Few trials measured oxidative stress directly; any benefit is expected to follow weight loss.

key_numbers.label: Weight change at 6 months (vs -5.6 kg continuous)
Hypoglycaemia rate ratio on glucose-lowering drugs

factors.name: Prolonged (multi-day) fasting
factors.headline: Fasts of 2-10+ days push ketones into the millimolar range and lowered lipid peroxidation (TBARS) in uncontrolled cohorts, but half or more of the weight lost is lean tissue and water, uric acid rises 100-200 umol/L, and no controlled trial shows lasting oxidative stress or health benefit beyond weight loss.

dose.effective: No proven effective dose. Medically supervised Buchinger-type fasts of 5-10 days at 200-250 kcal/day, or water-only fasts, have been studied; a refeeding period of at least half the fast length is used in clinics.
dose.studied_range: 2-21 days, water-only or 75-250 kcal/day, usually 1-2 times per year.
dose.too_much: Beyond ~5 days of little or no intake, refeeding-syndrome criteria apply (NICE: >5 days plus another risk factor, or >10 days alone). Risks: hyponatraemia, orthostatic hypotension, arrhythmia, gout and urate stones, gallstones, lean-mass loss. Never unsupervised with diabetes medication, low BMI, eating disorder, pregnancy, gout or kidney disease.
dose.timeframe: Ketosis from day 2-4; systemic proteome changes appear only after ~3 days; most weight is regained within weeks.
dose.notes: Ketonaemia reaches roughly 2-4 mmol/L by day 3-5 in many adults (higher in lean people and with exercise) and keeps rising for ~2-3 weeks.

factors.mechanism: Glycogen depletion (largely by ~24-42 h), lipolysis and ketogenesis; insulin and IGF-1 fall, growth hormone rises ~5-fold. Beta-hydroxybutyrate signalling (HDAC inhibition) and lower substrate flux may reduce ROS production; the rise in uric acid, an antioxidant, inflates total antioxidant capacity readings.
factors.interactions: Exercise during a fast speeds ketosis; light activity was used to protect muscle in the 10-day trial. Does not replace sustained [diet-calorie-restriction] or [weight-loss]. Avoid stacking with [vigorous-exercise-low-energy] in women.
factors.caveats: Evidence comes mostly from clinic cohorts run by fasting-clinic staff, without control groups. 'Autophagy peaks at day 2-3' is extrapolated from mice; human muscle and blood studies show ambiguous flux changes. TAC increases partly reflect uric acid.

key_numbers.label: Share of 10-day weight loss that was lean soft tissue

factors.name: Fasting-mimicking diet (5-day low-calorie, low-protein cycles)
factors.headline: Three monthly 5-day cycles (~1,100 then ~700 kcal/day, low protein) lowered weight, trunk fat, blood pressure and IGF-1 vs usual diet in one 100-person trial; no direct oxidative stress endpoints, and the lead developer holds a commercial interest.

dose.effective: 5 consecutive days per month of a plant-based, low-protein, low-sugar, higher-unsaturated-fat diet (~1,100 kcal on day 1, ~700 kcal on days 2-5), for 3 cycles.
dose.studied_range: 3 monthly cycles in generally healthy adults; 3 cycles over 4 months in men with poor semen quality.
dose.too_much: Same exclusions as fasting: pregnancy, eating disorders, underweight, diabetes medication without supervision.
dose.timeframe: Changes measured after 3 cycles (3 months).
dose.notes: Benefits were concentrated in people with elevated baseline risk; low protein is probably what lowers IGF-1.

factors.mechanism: Mimics fasting signals (low insulin, IGF-1 and amino acids) while supplying some food; in mice, cycles triggered regeneration on refeeding and extended lifespan.
factors.interactions: Effects overlap with [weight-loss]; IGF-1 lowering is also achieved by moderate protein reduction under [diet-calorie-restriction].
factors.caveats: Small number of trials, largely from one group with a commercial product; the 2.5-year 'biological age' reduction is an exploratory secondary analysis.

factors.name: MIND diet (Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay)
factors.headline: Cohort studies linked high MIND-diet adherence to 53% lower Alzheimer incidence, but the 3-year randomized MIND trial (604 people) found no cognitive or brain-MRI benefit over a control diet with the same mild calorie restriction.

dose.effective: The MIND score rewards green leafy vegetables, other vegetables, berries, nuts, olive oil, whole grains, fish, beans and poultry, and penalizes red meat, butter and margarine, cheese, pastries and sweets, and fried or fast food.
dose.studied_range: Trial: MIND diet with mild caloric restriction versus a control diet with the same mild caloric restriction, 3 years, cognitively healthy adults 65+ with a family history of dementia. Cohorts: 4.5-12 years of follow-up.
dose.timeframe: No difference detectable after 3 years in the trial.
dose.notes: Both trial groups improved, so the trial compared MIND with another calorie-restricted diet, not with an unchanged diet.

factors.mechanism: Proposed: polyphenols (berries, leafy greens), folate, vitamin E, carotenoids and omega-3 fats limit neuronal lipid peroxidation and neuroinflammation and support vascular health; less saturated fat and fried food reduce dietary oxidation products and cardiometabolic risk.
factors.interactions: A hybrid of [mediterranean-diet] and [dash-diet]; emphasizes [blueberries] and [leafy-greens]. Weight loss and calorie restriction were confounded with diet in the trial.
factors.caveats: The observational evidence comes from food-frequency questionnaires in health-conscious cohorts and is prone to confounding and reverse causation (people in early cognitive decline change their diets). The MIND score was derived and first tested in the same cohort.
factors.debate: For: the original Rush cohort [skb-morris2015] and an Australian cohort [skb-hosking2019] found lower risk with high adherence, and a Mediterranean-diet RCT substudy improved cognitive composites [skb-vallspedret2015]. Against: the MIND RCT was null [skb-barnes2023], and a 20-year Swedish cohort of 28,025 people found no link between midlife diet quality (including Mediterranean adherence) and dementia [skb-glans2023]. Defenders argue 3 years is too short and the control group also improved its diet; critics reply that this is exactly why observational associations should not be read as causal.

factors.name: Organic food (lower pesticide residues)
factors.headline: Switching to organic food reliably cuts urinary pesticide metabolites within days (e.g. organophosphate metabolites down ~60-95%), but health benefits rest on observational cohorts (25% lower cancer in high organic consumers, absolute difference 0.6%) that are heavily confounded.

dose.effective: If budget allows, prioritize organic versions of produce that typically carry high residues; never eat less fruit and vegetables to avoid pesticides.
dose.studied_range: Organic-diet interventions of about 1 week (urinary biomarkers); cohort comparisons of habitual organic intake.
dose.timeframe: Urinary metabolites fall within days; any disease effect would take years and is unproven.
dose.notes: Glyphosate fell with organic food only in people living away from fields; near farms, spray drift dominates.

factors.mechanism: Lowers dietary intake of organophosphate, pyrethroid and neonicotinoid residues, which in animals induce oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation and endocrine disruption.
factors.interactions: Sperm-specific pesticide data are in [pesticides]; fertility diet patterns that favour low-residue produce are in [profertility-diet]. Overall produce intake ([high-fruit-vegetable-intake]) matters more than its organic status.
factors.caveats: Organic buyers are richer, leaner, more active and eat better diets; cohort adjustment cannot remove all of this. No long-term randomized trial with clinical outcomes exists.
factors.debate: Exposure: organic-diet trials consistently lower urinary pesticide metabolites [env-hyland2019, env-gonzalez2023], though glyphosate fell only modestly [env-hyland2023]. Outcomes: NutriNet-Sante linked high organic intake to 25% lower cancer risk [env-baudry2018] and organic produce substitution to lower postmenopausal breast cancer only [env-berlivet2026], but an accompanying commentary questioned whether this justifies the cost [env-hemler2018]. Reviews split: one reports lower cardiometabolic risk in prospective studies [env-poulia2025], another finds data too contradictory for any conclusion [env-komati2025]. Fertility: high-residue produce was linked to 26% lower IVF live birth in women [env-chiu2018] and lower fertilization in male partners [env-kazemi2025], but a 5,234-woman preconception cohort found no link with natural fecundability and evidence of reverse causation [env-wesselink2020].

factors.name: Unneeded iron supplements / excess iron intake
factors.headline: Iron pills taken without a deficiency mostly pass unabsorbed into the colon, where 19 mg/day raised faecal free-radical production by ~40% and, in infant trials, shifted gut bacteria toward pathogens and inflammation; genetic studies link lifelong higher iron to shorter lifespan and more diabetes.

dose.effective: Take iron only to correct documented deficiency (ferritin below ~30 ug/L, or below ~50 ug/L with symptoms such as fatigue), then stop or reduce once ferritin is replete. Most iron-replete men and postmenopausal women need no supplemental iron; a multivitamin 'for men' or '50+' formula without iron is the sensible default.
dose.studied_range: 19 mg/day ferrous sulfate for 2 weeks (adults, gut markers); 2.5-12.5 mg/day in infant micronutrient powders; >100 mg/day high-dose supplements (cross-sectional microbiome data).
dose.too_much: IOM UL 45 mg/day elemental iron (GI side effects); EFSA set no UL but a safe level of 40 mg/day total iron for adults including pregnancy. Untargeted iron in malaria-endemic settings raised severe illness and death in young children. Never self-supplement with known or suspected haemochromatosis.
dose.timeframe: Gut changes within 2 weeks; systemic store build-up over years.
dose.notes: Absorption is regulated (hepcidin) but there is no excretion route, so stores accumulate in iron-replete people, especially men. Vitamin C taken with iron raises non-heme absorption; tea, coffee and calcium lower it.

factors.mechanism: Unabsorbed ferrous iron in the colon catalyses Fenton chemistry (Fe2+ + H2O2 -> hydroxyl radical) and lipid peroxidation, and favours iron-hungry Enterobacteriaceae over bifidobacteria and butyrate producers. Systemically, surplus iron expands the labile iron pool that feeds Fenton reactions and ferroptosis.
factors.interactions: Heme iron from red and processed meat acts similarly in the gut [processed-red-meat]. Do not pair high-dose vitamin C with iron in people with high stores [vitamin-c-status]. Overlaps with [iron-status-ferritin]; the opposite risk is [iron-deficiency]. Multivitamins often contain 8-18 mg iron [multivitamin-mineral].
factors.caveats: Faecal radical generation is an ex vivo assay and the infant microbiome trials were done in low-income settings with high pathogen loads; adult outcome data are thin. The harm signal is for iron the body does not need: in deficient people, including many pregnant women, iron is clearly beneficial.
factors.debate: Harm from untargeted iron is shown by infant trials (Pemba mortality [nut-sazawal2006]; Kenyan microbiome and calprotectin [nut-jaeggi2015]) and by gut-biology commentaries [nut-weiss2015, nut-simonytesjodin2019], with Mendelian randomization suggesting lifelong higher iron shortens lifespan [nut-daghlas2021]. On the other side, a 2023 meta-analysis found daily iron in iron-replete pregnant women still reduced iron-deficiency anaemia and low birthweight [nut-hansen2023], and EFSA could not identify a dose-response for chronic disease, setting only a conservative safe level [nut-efsa2024iron]. Adult evidence for harm at typical multivitamin doses (8-18 mg) is lacking.

mechanisms.name: Nrf2 / KEAP1 pathway
mechanisms.description: Electrophiles such as sulforaphane (and, more weakly, curcumin, garlic sulfur compounds and some coffee roast products) modify cysteines on KEAP1, so Nrf2 escapes degradation and switches on glutathione synthesis, GSTs, NQO1, HO-1 and other cytoprotective enzymes. These 'indirect antioxidants' act catalytically and for longer than the inducer stays in blood. Induction is bounded (enzyme levels plateau) and human dose-response curves are poorly mapped; no maximally effective dose has been established.

mechanisms.name: Direct radical scavenging (and why it mostly fails in vivo)
mechanisms.description: Polyphenols scavenge radicals in test tubes (ORAC, FRAP, Folin), but in the body they are present at low micromolar or lower concentrations, mostly as conjugates and microbial metabolites, and cannot out-compete endogenous enzymes kinetically. Plausible exceptions are inside the gut lumen and food itself, where concentrations are high (e.g. spices preventing lipid oxidation in meat), and lipid-soluble carotenoids/tocopherols and vitamin C, which are real chain-breaking antioxidants up to saturation.

mechanisms.name: NADPH oxidase and postprandial oxidative stress
mechanisms.description: Large meals, glucose, fat and AGEs acutely upregulate leukocyte and vascular NADPH oxidase, raising superoxide for several hours. Blueberry metabolites lowered neutrophil NADPH oxidase activity in parallel with improved vascular function.

mechanisms.name: Endothelial nitric oxide
mechanisms.description: Flavanols, anthocyanin metabolites and dietary nitrate raise nitric-oxide bioavailability; flow-mediated dilation (FMD) is the most reproducible human outcome for polyphenol foods and partly reflects reduced vascular superoxide.

mechanisms.name: Gut microbial metabolism of polyphenols
mechanisms.description: Most anthocyanins, flavan-3-ol oligomers, chlorogenic acids and ellagitannins reach the colon, where bacteria convert them into phenolic acids, valerolactones and urolithins that circulate for up to 48 h. Inter-individual differences in this metabolism are large and partly explain variable responses.

mechanisms.name: Glycation and dietary AGEs
mechanisms.description: Dry-heat cooking of protein- and fat-rich foods creates AGEs; hyperglycemia also forms them endogenously. AGE-RAGE signalling activates NADPH oxidase and NF-kB.

mechanisms.name: Iron and Fenton chemistry
mechanisms.description: Free or heme iron catalyses hydroxyl radical formation and lipid peroxidation, notably in the gut after red meat or unneeded iron supplements.

mechanisms.name: Mitochondrial ROS from nutrient excess
mechanisms.description: Overfeeding increases electron supply to the respiratory chain and superoxide leak; calorie restriction does the reverse.

mechanisms.name: Hormesis / para-hormesis
mechanisms.description: Mild electrophilic or oxidative signals (from phytochemicals, exercise, fasting) upregulate endogenous defences; high-dose direct antioxidants can blunt such signals, as vitamin C + E blunted exercise-induced gains in insulin sensitivity.

mechanisms.name: Inflammation / NF-kB
mechanisms.description: Oxidized dietary lipids, AGEs, excess nutrients and trans fats activate NF-kB-driven inflammation, which itself generates ROS; olive phenolics, fiber-derived SCFA and weight loss dampen it.

mechanisms.name: How oxidative stress is measured in diet trials
mechanisms.description: Validation work found plasma/urinary F2-isoprostanes and MDA measured by mass spectrometry, and urinary 8-OHdG, to be the most reliable general markers; TBARS, 'total antioxidant capacity' (TAC, FRAP, ORAC of plasma) and many ELISA kits are non-specific. Even 8-iso-PGF2alpha can rise from enzymatic COX activity during inflammation. Many positive food trials rely on the weaker markers.

references.finding: Curcuma domestica extract 1500 mg/day was non-inferior to ibuprofen 1200 mg/day over 4 weeks on WOMAC, with fewer abdominal complaints.

references.authors: Kusuhara H, Furuie H, Inano A, et al.
references.title: Pharmacokinetic interaction study of sulphasalazine in healthy subjects and the impact of curcumin as an in vivo inhibitor of BCRP.
references.finding: 2 g curcumin inhibited intestinal BCRP and raised sulfasalazine exposure 2.0-3.2-fold in humans.

references.authors: Lombardi N, Crescioli G, Maggini V, et al.
references.title: Acute liver injury following turmeric use in Tuscany: An analysis of the Italian Phytovigilance database and systematic review of case reports.
references.finding: Italian phytovigilance cases of acute (mostly cholestatic) hepatitis were all linked to high-bioavailability, high-dose curcumin products; positive dechallenge in most.

references.authors: Mahale J, Singh R, Howells LM, et al.
references.title: Detection of Plasma Curcuminoids from Dietary Intake of Turmeric-Containing Food in Human Volunteers.
references.finding: After a turmeric-containing meal at South Asian culinary levels, curcumin glucuronide peaked at ~48 nM and free curcumin was detectable (3.2 nM) in only one volunteer.

references.authors: Menniti-Ippolito F, Ippoliti I, Pastorelli AA, et al.
references.title: Turmeric (Curcuma longa L.) food supplements and hepatotoxicity: an integrated evaluation approach.
references.finding: A 2019 Italian cluster of 28 acute hepatitis reports linked to turmeric supplements; product testing looked for drugs, metals, aflatoxins, dyes and pyrrolizidine alkaloids, and regulators intervened.

references.authors: Musso G, Pinach S, Mariano F, et al.
references.title: Effect of phospholipid curcumin Meriva on liver histology and kidney disease in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
references.finding: Meriva 2 g/day for 72 weeks: NASH resolution in 62% vs 12% on placebo and fibrosis improvement in 50% vs 8%; single trial, needs replication.

references.authors: Nelson KM, Dahlin JL, Bisson J, et al.
references.title: The Essential Medicinal Chemistry of Curcumin.
references.finding: Argues curcumin is a PAINS/IMPS compound that is chemically unstable, reactive and not bioavailable; states that no double-blind placebo-controlled curcumin trial had been successful as of 2017.

references.authors: Ng TP, Chiam PC, Lee T, et al.
references.title: Curry consumption and cognitive function in the elderly.
references.finding: Occasional or frequent curry eaters had better MMSE scores than never/rare eaters (cross-sectional association, confounding possible).

references.authors: Pal A, Sung B, Bhanu Prasad BA, et al.
references.title: Curcumin glucuronides: assessing the proliferative activity against human cell lines.
references.finding: Curcumin killed cancer cell lines at 1-10 uM, but its mono- and di-glucuronides (the main circulating forms) showed no antiproliferative activity.

references.authors: Pattanaik S, Hota D, Prabhakar S, et al.
references.title: Effect of piperine on the steady-state pharmacokinetics of phenytoin in patients with epilepsy.
references.finding: A single 20 mg piperine dose significantly raised phenytoin AUC and Cmax at steady state.

references.authors: US National Library of Medicine
references.title: PubMed searches 'Aggarwal BB[au] AND retracted publication[pt]' and 'curcumin AND retracted publication[pt]', run 2026-10-01 via NCBI E-utilities.
references.finding: Returned 27 retracted publications with BB Aggarwal as author and 162 retracted publications mentioning curcumin.

references.authors: Purpura M, Lowery RP, Wilson JM, et al.
references.title: Analysis of different innovative formulations of curcumin for improved relative oral bioavailability in human subjects.
references.finding: A gamma-cyclodextrin curcumin complex gave 39-fold higher total curcuminoid AUC than unformulated extract, exceeding a phytosome and a turmeric-oil formulation.

references.authors: Qin S, Huang L, Gong J, et al.
references.title: Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials of 4 weeks or longer suggest that curcumin may afford some protection against oxidative stress.
references.finding: Curcumin >=4 weeks lowered MDA (SMD -0.77) and raised SOD (SMD 1.08) with no change in RBC GPx; the MDA effect appeared at >=600 mg/day curcuminoids.

references.authors: Rasyid A, Rahman AR, Jaalam K, et al.
references.title: Effect of different curcumin dosages on human gall bladder.
references.finding: Curcumin 20, 40 and 80 mg contracted the gallbladder by 34%, 51% and 72% within 2 h.

references.authors: Ringman JM, Frautschy SA, Teng E, et al.
references.title: Oral curcumin for Alzheimer's disease: tolerability and efficacy in a 24-week randomized, double blind, placebo-controlled study.
references.finding: Curcumin C3 Complex 2 or 4 g/day for 24 weeks showed no clinical or biomarker benefit; native plasma curcumin was low (7.3 ng/mL) and 3 withdrew for GI symptoms.

references.authors: Ristow M, Zarse K, Oberbach A, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants prevent health-promoting effects of physical exercise in humans.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Vitamin C 1000 mg plus vitamin E 400 IU/day blocked exercise-induced gains in insulin sensitivity and induction of endogenous antioxidant defences.

references.authors: Ryan Wolf J, Heckler CE, Guido JJ, et al.
references.title: Oral curcumin for radiation dermatitis: a URCC NCORP study of 686 breast cancer patients.
references.finding: Oral curcumin 6 g/day during radiotherapy did not reduce radiation dermatitis severity versus placebo.

references.authors: Schiborr C, Kocher A, Behnam D, et al.
references.title: The oral bioavailability of curcumin from micronized powder and liquid micelles is significantly increased in healthy humans and differs between sexes.
references.finding: Single 500 mg dose: micronized curcumin was 9-fold and liquid micellar curcumin 185-fold more bioavailable (AUC) than native powder; women absorbed more than men.

references.authors: Shin JW, Chun KS, Kim DH, et al.
references.title: Curcumin induces stabilization of Nrf2 protein through Keap1 cysteine modification.
references.finding: In mouse skin and epidermal cells, curcumin binds KEAP1 Cys151 and stabilises Nrf2 to induce HO-1; tetrahydrocurcumin, which lacks the Michael-acceptor group, does not.

references.authors: Shoba G, Joy D, Joseph T, et al.
references.title: Influence of piperine on the pharmacokinetics of curcumin in animals and human volunteers.
references.finding: 2 g curcumin alone gave undetectable or very low serum levels; with 20 mg piperine bioavailability (AUC) rose about 2000%.

references.authors: Small GW, Siddarth P, Li Z, et al.
references.title: Memory and Brain Amyloid and Tau Effects of a Bioavailable Form of Curcumin in Non-Demented Adults: A Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled 18-Month Trial.
references.finding: Theracurmin 90 mg curcumin twice daily for 18 months improved verbal and visual memory and attention versus placebo and lowered FDDNP-PET signal in amygdala/hypothalamus; very small trial.

references.authors: Stohs SJ, Chen CYO, Preuss HG, et al.
references.title: The fallacy of enzymatic hydrolysis for the determination of bioactive curcumin in plasma samples as an indication of bioavailability: a comparative study.
references.finding: Most curcumin PK studies hydrolyse plasma before analysis and so report total (free plus conjugated) curcumin, which overstates the bioactive free fraction.

references.authors: Tang M, Larson-Meyer DE, Liebman M
references.title: Effect of cinnamon and turmeric on urinary oxalate excretion, plasma lipids, and plasma glucose in healthy subjects.
references.finding: Supplemental turmeric raised urinary oxalate excretion (91% of its oxalate is soluble) and did not change glucose or lipids over 4 weeks.

references.authors: Tayyem RF, Heath DD, Al-Delaimy WK, et al.
references.title: Curcumin content of turmeric and curry powders.
references.finding: HPLC of 28 spice products: pure turmeric powder averaged 3.14% curcumin by weight; most curry powders contained little and variable curcumin.

references.authors: Tuntipopipat S, Judprasong K, Zeder C, et al.
references.title: Chili, but not turmeric, inhibits iron absorption in young women from an iron-fortified composite meal.
references.finding: 0.5 g turmeric in a meal did not inhibit iron absorption (stable isotopes), whereas chili cut it by 38%.

references.authors: Vareed SK, Kakarala M, Ruffin MT, et al.
references.title: Pharmacokinetics of curcumin conjugate metabolites in healthy human subjects.
references.finding: After 10 or 12 g curcumin, free curcumin was detectable in only one subject; glucuronide and sulfate conjugates were found in all (Cmax ~1.7-2.3 ug/mL).

references.authors: Wang Z, Jones G, Winzenberg T, et al.
references.title: Effectiveness of Curcuma longa Extract for the Treatment of Symptoms and Effusion-Synovitis of Knee Osteoarthritis : A Randomized Trial.
references.n: 70 adults with knee OA and effusion-synovitis
references.finding: Curcuma longa extract (2 capsules/day, 12 weeks) cut VAS knee pain by 9.1 mm versus placebo but did not change effusion-synovitis volume or cartilage; funded partly by the manufacturer.

references.authors: Wang Z, Singh A, Jones G, et al.
references.title: Efficacy and Safety of Turmeric Extracts for the Treatment of Knee Osteoarthritis: a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials.
references.finding: Turmeric extracts reduced knee OA pain (SMD -0.82) and improved function versus placebo, similar to NSAIDs; very high heterogeneity, moderate risk of bias, less benefit with higher BMI.

references.authors: Alumkal JJ, Slottke R, Schwartzman J, et al.
references.title: A phase II study of sulforaphane-rich broccoli sprout extracts in men with recurrent prostate cancer.
references.n: 20 men with recurrent prostate cancer (single arm)
references.finding: 200 µmol/day sulforaphane-rich extract for up to 20 weeks did not produce >=50% PSA declines (1 of 20), but PSA doubling time lengthened from 6.1 to 9.6 months.

references.authors: Armah CN, Derdemezis C, Traka MH, et al.
references.title: Diet rich in high glucoraphanin broccoli reduces plasma LDL cholesterol: Evidence from randomised controlled trials.
references.finding: 400 g/week of high-glucoraphanin broccoli for 12 weeks lowered LDL cholesterol by 5-7%, more than standard broccoli (2-3%, not significant).

references.authors: Atwell LL, Hsu A, Wong CP, et al.
references.title: Absorption and chemopreventive targets of sulforaphane in humans following consumption of broccoli sprouts or a myrosinase-treated broccoli sprout extract.
references.finding: At 200 µmol/day, fresh sprouts gave ~3x higher sulforaphane metabolites than a myrosinase-treated extract; splitting the dose prolonged exposure; no dose response in HO-1, HDAC activity or p21.

references.authors: Aune D, Giovannucci E, Boffetta P, et al.
references.title: Fruit and vegetable intake and the risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer and all-cause mortality-a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies.
references.finding: Per 200 g/day fruit and vegetables, all-cause mortality RR 0.90; cruciferous vegetables were among the types most strongly inversely associated with outcomes.

references.authors: Axelsson AS, Tubbs E, Mecham B, et al.
references.title: Sulforaphane reduces hepatic glucose production and improves glucose control in patients with type 2 diabetes.
references.finding: Broccoli sprout extract (150 µmol sulforaphane/day, 12 weeks) reduced fasting blood glucose and HbA1c in obese patients with dysregulated type 2 diabetes (not in the whole group); in cells and animals sulforaphane suppressed hepatic gluconeogenesis via NRF2.

references.authors: Bahadoran Z, Mirmiran P, Hosseinpanah F, et al.
references.title: Broccoli sprouts reduce oxidative stress in type 2 diabetes: a randomized double-blind clinical trial.
references.finding: 5-10 g/day broccoli sprout powder for 4 weeks lowered MDA, oxidized LDL and an oxidative stress index and raised total antioxidant capacity.

references.authors: Charron CS, Vinyard BT, Ross SA, et al.
references.title: Absorption and metabolism of isothiocyanates formed from broccoli glucosinolates: effects of BMI and daily consumption in a randomised clinical trial.
references.finding: Fifteen days of daily broccoli did not uniformly change isothiocyanate absorption: it rose in leaner people (BMI <26) and fell in heavier people; GSTM1 genotype had no effect.

references.authors: Chartoumpekis DV, Ziros PG, Chen JG, et al.
references.title: Broccoli sprout beverage is safe for thyroid hormonal and autoimmune status: Results of a 12-week randomized trial.
references.finding: 84 days of a sulforaphane/glucoraphanin beverage did not change TSH, free T4, thyroglobulin or thyroid autoimmunity.

references.authors: Chen JG, Johnson J, Egner P, et al.
references.title: Dose-dependent detoxication of the airborne pollutant benzene in a randomized trial of broccoli sprout beverage in Qidong, China.
references.finding: Only the full-dose beverage (median 24.6 µmol urinary sulforaphane metabolites/day) raised benzene mercapturic acid (+63%); half (+11%) and one-fifth (-6%) doses did not differ from placebo.

references.authors: Cipolla BG, Mandron E, Lefort JM, et al.
references.title: Effect of Sulforaphane in Men with Biochemical Recurrence after Radical Prostatectomy.
references.finding: 60 mg (~340 µmol) stabilised sulforaphane daily for 6 months missed the primary PSA-slope endpoint; PSA rose less (+0.10 vs +0.62 ng/mL) and doubling time was 86% longer than placebo.

references.authors: Clarke JD, Hsu A, Riedl K, et al.
references.title: Bioavailability and inter-conversion of sulforaphane and erucin in human subjects consuming broccoli sprouts or broccoli supplement in a cross-over study design.
references.finding: A myrosinase-free broccoli supplement produced dramatically lower and later plasma and urinary sulforaphane and erucin than 40 g fresh broccoli sprouts.

references.authors: Clarke JD, Riedl K, Bella D, et al.
references.title: Comparison of isothiocyanate metabolite levels and histone deacetylase activity in human subjects consuming broccoli sprouts or broccoli supplement.
references.finding: Fresh sprouts gave higher, earlier isothiocyanate excretion than a myrosinase-free supplement with equal glucosinolate, and only sprouts lowered blood-cell HDAC activity.

references.authors: Conaway CC, Getahun SM, Liebes LL, et al.
references.title: Disposition of glucosinolates and sulforaphane in humans after ingestion of steamed and fresh broccoli.
references.finding: After 200 g broccoli, 32% of isothiocyanates were excreted from fresh vs 10% from steamed broccoli, a roughly 3-fold difference.

references.authors: Cramer JM, Teran-Garcia M, Jeffery EH
references.title: Enhancing sulforaphane absorption and excretion in healthy men through the combined consumption of fresh broccoli sprouts and a glucoraphanin-rich powder.
references.finding: Combining fresh sprouts (70 µmol) with a myrosinase-free glucoraphanin powder recovered 65% of the dose as urinary SF-NAC vs 60% for sprouts alone and 24% for the powder alone.

references.authors: Cuadrado A, Rojo AI, Wells G, et al.
references.title: Therapeutic targeting of the NRF2 and KEAP1 partnership in chronic diseases.
references.finding: NRF2 activation is cytoprotective in many chronic disease models, but target specificity, pharmacodynamics, efficacy and safety remain unresolved challenges for therapeutic activators.

references.authors: de Zeeuw D, Akizawa T, Audhya P, et al.
references.title: Bardoxolone methyl in type 2 diabetes and stage 4 chronic kidney disease.
references.finding: The synthetic Nrf2 activator bardoxolone methyl did not reduce kidney failure or CV death and increased heart-failure events (HR 1.83); the trial was stopped early.

references.authors: Dickerson F, Origoni A, Katsafanas E, et al.
references.title: Randomized controlled trial of an adjunctive sulforaphane nutraceutical in schizophrenia.
references.finding: 100 µmol/day adjunctive sulforaphane for 18 weeks had no significant effect on symptoms or cognition (as summarised by a 2025 meta-analysis).

references.authors: Dinkova-Kostova AT, Holtzclaw WD, Cole RN, et al.
references.title: Direct evidence that sulfhydryl groups of Keap1 are the sensors regulating induction of phase 2 enzymes that protect against carcinogens and oxidants.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Showed directly that inducers such as sulforaphane react with the most reactive of KEAP1's 25 cysteine thiols, disrupting the KEAP1-Nrf2 complex so Nrf2 can activate ARE-driven genes.

references.authors: Duran CG, Burbank AJ, Mills KH, et al.
references.title: A proof-of-concept clinical study examining the NRF2 activator sulforaphane against neutrophilic airway inflammation.
references.finding: Broccoli sprout homogenate did not induce antioxidant genes or protect against neutrophilic airway inflammation after ozone exposure.

references.authors: Dwibedi C, Axelsson AS, Abrahamsson B, et al.
references.title: Effect of broccoli sprout extract and baseline gut microbiota on fasting blood glucose in prediabetes: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial.
references.finding: 150 µmol/day broccoli sprout extract for 12 weeks missed its primary target (fasting glucose -0.2 mmol/L vs placebo, P=0.04); responders had gut Bacteroides genes for glucoraphanin conversion; GI side effects were more common.

references.authors: Egner PA, Chen JG, Wang JB, et al.
references.title: Bioavailability of Sulforaphane from two broccoli sprout beverages: results of a short-term, cross-over clinical trial in Qidong, China.
references.finding: A sulforaphane-rich beverage gave ~70% urinary recovery vs ~5% for a glucoraphanin-rich beverage, with less inter-individual variation; glucoraphanin gave slower, steadier exposure.

references.authors: Egner PA, Chen JG, Zarth AT, et al.
references.title: Rapid and sustainable detoxication of airborne pollutants by broccoli sprout beverage: results of a randomized clinical trial in China.
references.finding: Daily 600 µmol glucoraphanin + 40 µmol sulforaphane for 12 weeks raised excretion of benzene (+61%) and acrolein (+23%) conjugates vs placebo; sulforaphane bioavailability did not decline over 12 weeks.

references.authors: Fahey JW, Zhang Y, Talalay P
references.title: Broccoli sprouts: an exceptionally rich source of inducers of enzymes that protect against chemical carcinogens.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Three-day-old broccoli sprouts contain 10-100 times more glucoraphanin than mature plants and negligible indole glucosinolates; sprout extracts reduced DMBA mammary tumours in rats.

references.authors: Fahey JW, Wehage SL, Holtzclaw WD, et al.
references.title: Protection of humans by plant glucosinolates: efficiency of conversion of glucosinolates to isothiocyanates by the gastrointestinal microflora.
references.finding: Gut-microbial conversion of glucoraphanin varied from ~1% to >40% between people but was consistent within a person; preformed isothiocyanates gave 70-90%; antibiotics and bowel cleansing abolish conversion.

references.authors: Fahey JW, Holtzclaw WD, Wehage SL, et al.
references.title: Sulforaphane Bioavailability from Glucoraphanin-Rich Broccoli: Control by Active Endogenous Myrosinase.
references.finding: Sprouts or seeds given with their own active myrosinase yielded 3-4x more sulforaphane than glucoraphanin without active myrosinase; a commercial glucoraphanin supplement matched a boiled sprout extract.

references.authors: Fahey JW, Wade KL, Wehage SL, et al.
references.title: Stabilized sulforaphane for clinical use: Phytochemical delivery efficiency.
references.finding: Stabilised sulforaphane preparations (cyclodextrin and a commercial supplement) were as bioavailable as pure sulforaphane, peaking at about 2 h, but 6 of 10 volunteers reported mild stomach upset with one form.

references.authors: Fahey JW, Wade KL, Stephenson KK, et al.
references.title: Bioavailability of Sulforaphane Following Ingestion of Glucoraphanin-Rich Broccoli Sprout and Seed Extracts with Active Myrosinase: A Pilot Study of the Effects of Proton Pump Inhibitor Administration.
references.finding: With a glucoraphanin plus active-myrosinase seed/sprout extract, omeprazole (less stomach acid) and enteric coating increased conversion; greater body mass reduced conversion; cytoprotective PBMC genes rose with bioavailability.

references.authors: Felker P, Bunch R, Leung AM
references.title: Concentrations of thiocyanate and goitrin in human plasma, their precursor concentrations in brassica vegetables, and associated potential risk for hypothyroidism.
references.finding: Goitrin inhibits thyroid iodine uptake at 194 but not 77 µmol; collards, Brussels sprouts and some Russian kale can contain that much, while commercial broccoli and kale contain <10 µmol per 100 g.

references.authors: Galanty A, Grudzińska M, Paździora W, et al.
references.title: Do Brassica Vegetables Affect Thyroid Function?-A Comprehensive Systematic Review.
references.finding: Systematic review: most evidence does not support antithyroid effects of Brassica vegetables in humans, especially with adequate iodine intake.

references.authors: Gasper AV, Al-Janobi A, Smith JA, et al.
references.title: Glutathione S-transferase M1 polymorphism and metabolism of sulforaphane from standard and high-glucosinolate broccoli.
references.finding: GSTM1-null people had slightly higher plasma sulforaphane AUC and faster, larger urinary excretion than GSTM1-positive people; high-glucosinolate broccoli gave ~3x more sulforaphane.

references.authors: Houghton CA, Fassett RG, Coombes JS
references.title: Sulforaphane and Other Nutrigenomic Nrf2 Activators: Can the Clinician's Expectation Be Matched by the Reality?
references.finding: Sulforaphane activates Nrf2 more potently and is far more bioavailable than curcumin, silymarin or resveratrol supplements.

references.authors: Hu C, Eggler AL, Mesecar AD, et al.
references.title: Modification of keap1 cysteine residues by sulforaphane.
references.finding: Mass spectrometry with a corrected protocol confirmed that KEAP1 cysteine 151 is among the residues most readily (and reversibly) modified by sulforaphane.

references.authors: Kassar O, M Mansour ME, Farag N, et al.
references.title: Efficacy and safety of sulforaphane in schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
references.finding: Sulforaphane did not improve PANSS total or positive scores; a small negative-symptom benefit at 12 weeks (MD -1.06) was not sustained; lipids improved and discontinuation was lower.

references.authors: Kensler TW, Chen JG, Egner PA, et al.
references.title: Effects of glucosinolate-rich broccoli sprouts on urinary levels of aflatoxin-DNA adducts and phenanthrene tetraols in a randomized clinical trial in He Zuo township, Qidong, People's Republic of China.
references.finding: Nightly broccoli sprout infusion (400 µmol glucoraphanin) for 2 weeks did not change aflatoxin-DNA adducts between arms, but higher sulforaphane excretion correlated with fewer adducts and phenanthrene tetraols.

references.authors: Kensler TW, Ng D, Carmella SG, et al.
references.title: Modulation of the metabolism of airborne pollutants by glucoraphanin-rich and sulforaphane-rich broccoli sprout beverages in Qidong, China.
references.finding: Seven days of sulforaphane-rich or glucoraphanin-rich sprout beverage raised excretion of glutathione conjugates of acrolein, crotonaldehyde and benzene by 20-50% vs baseline, with no difference between beverages.

references.authors: Kikuchi M, Ushida Y, Shiozawa H, et al.
references.title: Sulforaphane-rich broccoli sprout extract improves hepatic abnormalities in male subjects.
references.finding: Glucoraphanin-rich sprout extract capsules for 2 months lowered ALT, gamma-GTP and urinary 8-OHdG vs placebo.

references.authors: Li YZ, Yang ZY, Gong TT, et al.
references.title: Cruciferous vegetable consumption and multiple health outcomes: an umbrella review of 41 systematic reviews and meta-analyses of 303 observational studies.
references.finding: Umbrella review: cruciferous vegetable intake associated with lower risk of several cancers and all-cause mortality, but evidence was mostly weak to suggestive and observational.

references.authors: Liou CS, Sirk SJ, Diaz CAC, et al.
references.title: A Metabolic Pathway for Activation of Dietary Glucosinolates by a Human Gut Symbiont.
references.finding: Identified the Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron operon (BT2159-BT2156) that converts dietary glucosinolates to isothiocyanates in the gut.

references.authors: London SJ, Yuan JM, Chung FL, et al.
references.title: Isothiocyanates, glutathione S-transferase M1 and T1 polymorphisms, and lung-cancer risk: a prospective study of men in Shanghai, China.
references.finding: Detectable urinary isothiocyanates predicted lower lung cancer risk (RR 0.65), most strongly in GSTM1-null (RR 0.36) and GSTM1/GSTT1 double-null men (RR 0.28).

references.authors: López-Chillón MT, Carazo-Díaz C, Prieto-Merino D, et al.
references.title: Effects of long-term consumption of broccoli sprouts on inflammatory markers in overweight subjects.
references.finding: 30 g/day fresh broccoli sprouts for 10 weeks lowered IL-6 (4.76 to 2.11 pg/mL) and CRP in an uncontrolled before-after design.

references.authors: Lozanovski VJ, Polychronidis G, Gross W, et al.
references.title: Broccoli sprout supplementation in patients with advanced pancreatic cancer is difficult despite positive effects-results from the POUDER pilot study.
references.finding: Broccoli sprout capsules (508 µmol sulforaphane + 411 µmol glucoraphanin/day) were hard to tolerate (15 capsules, nausea, high drop-out); early survival trends favoured treatment but the pilot was underpowered.

references.authors: Magner M, Thorová K, Župová V, et al.
references.title: Sulforaphane Treatment in Children with Autism: A Prospective Randomized Double-Blind Study.
references.finding: 50 µmol/day sulforaphane for 36 weeks produced no significant improvement in ADOS-2, SRS-2 or ABC vs placebo.

references.authors: Mahéo K, Morel F, Langouët S, et al.
references.title: Inhibition of cytochromes P-450 and induction of glutathione S-transferases by sulforaphane in primary human and rat hepatocytes.
references.finding: In primary human hepatocytes, sulforaphane induced GSTA1/2 and markedly decreased CYP3A4 expression and activity, while CYP1A2 was unaffected.

references.authors: Mastaloudis A, Holcomb L, Fahey JW, et al.
references.title: Exogenous myrosinase from mustard seed increases bioavailability of sulforaphane from a glucoraphanin-rich broccoli seed extract in a randomized clinical study.
references.finding: Adding mustard-seed myrosinase to a glucoraphanin-rich broccoli seed extract doubled sulforaphane bioavailability (39.8% vs 18.6%); bacterial glucoraphanin-converting genes correlated with conversion.

references.authors: Matusheski NV, Juvik JA, Jeffery EH
references.title: Heating decreases epithiospecifier protein activity and increases sulforaphane formation in broccoli.
references.finding: Heating broccoli to 60 °C before crushing increased sulforaphane and decreased the inactive nitrile by inactivating epithiospecifier protein; 70 °C and above reduced both in florets.

references.authors: Myzak MC, Tong P, Dashwood WM, et al.
references.title: Sulforaphane retards the growth of human PC-3 xenografts and inhibits HDAC activity in human subjects.
references.finding: A single 68 g serving of broccoli sprouts inhibited histone deacetylase (HDAC) activity in blood mononuclear cells at 3 and 6 h; sulforaphane also slowed prostate cancer xenografts in mice.

references.authors: Navarro SL, Peterson S, Chen C, et al.
references.title: Cruciferous vegetable feeding alters UGT1A1 activity: diet- and genotype-dependent changes in serum bilirubin in a controlled feeding trial.
references.finding: Cruciferous vegetable diets lowered serum bilirubin vs a vegetable-free diet, indicating induction of the drug-conjugating enzyme UGT1A1.

references.authors: Navarro SL, Schwarz Y, Song X, et al.
references.title: Cruciferous vegetables have variable effects on biomarkers of systemic inflammation in a randomized controlled trial in healthy young adults.
references.finding: Double-dose crucifers (14 g/kg body weight) for 14 days lowered IL-6 by 19% vs a vegetable-free diet; no effect on CRP or TNF-alpha.

references.authors: Noah TL, Zhang H, Zhou H, et al.
references.title: Effect of broccoli sprouts on nasal response to live attenuated influenza virus in smokers: a randomized, double-blind study.
references.finding: Four days of broccoli sprout homogenate reduced post-vaccine nasal IL-6 and influenza virus quantity and raised NQO1 in smokers; trends in nonsmokers were not significant.

references.authors: Nouchi R, Hu Q, Ushida Y, et al.
references.title: Effects of sulforaphane intake on processing speed and negative moods in healthy older adults: Evidence from a randomized controlled trial.
